title: Korean marks: inscriptions on Goryeo, buncheong and Joseon ceramics, makers' marks since 1883, and how Korean dates are written
applies_to: Writing on Korean items: the government-office, palace-hall, place and character inscriptions on Goryeo celadon, buncheong and Joseon white porcelain; the marks of colonial-period workshops and of 20th-century makers and factories; and dates written in Korean eras, the Chongzhen count, Dangi years and cyclical years. A decode names what the writing names, and gives the year a written date states; it never says an item is of the period, because old inscriptions were copied on later wares.

caveats: An inscription names who or what a ware was made for, or by. It does not date the item or show that it is genuine: Goryeo celadon was reproduced under Japanese rule (1910–1945) and again from the 1950s, and old inscriptions can be copied.
Many entries rest on one museum's catalogue, or on one scholar's reading; the panel says so where that is the case, and gives every source.

Readings differ: catalogues transcribe or read the same inscription differently (金山 read as Gimsan, Geumsan or Busan; 三加 or 三嘉), and some offices' dates are disputed. The panel gives each reading with its source.
reading: Most Korean inscriptions are in hanja, the Chinese characters Korea wrote in until the 20th century; a few late Joseon items are in hangul. Read them as Chinese: an office's name (長興庫), a place and an office (慶州長興庫), a palace hall (中宮殿), a single character (天).

Buncheong for government use was stamped or inlaid with the receiving office's name from 1417, by royal order, so that items taken from the offices could be traced; many add the district that made them.
The court kilns at Gwangju marked white porcelain with single characters and cyclical years; in the 19th century, with the names of the palace halls it was made for.
A cyclical year written alone (庚午) comes round every sixty years: the date reader lists the years it could be.

groups.name: Goryeo celadon and other Goryeo wares
groups.blurb: Goryeo potters wrote little on their wares. What there is names the court office a ware was made for, gives a date, or carries a poem.

groups.name: Buncheong and early Joseon stoneware
groups.blurb: From 1417 wares made for the government offices had to carry the office's name, against theft; many also name the district that made them.

groups.name: Joseon white porcelain
groups.blurb: The court's own kilns at Gwangju marked their porcelain with single characters, cyclical years and, in the 19th century, the names of the palace halls it was made for.

groups.name: Since 1883: workshops, factories and makers
groups.blurb: Reproductions of Goryeo celadon made under Japanese rule, the royal household's workshop, and the celadon potters and factories whose marks are on the wares most often found in Western homes.

rows.meaning: Royal Pharmacy (Office of Royal Medicine), the Goryeo court office in charge of medicine
rows.technique: white inlay on one recorded box (Handok Museum); incised on another (National Museum of Korea)
rows.where_on_object: on the outer side of the lid and of the lower body, near where the two meet
rows.date_note: The surviving boxes are dated to the 12th century (heritage record) or the mid-12th century (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, from the jade-green glaze, quartz spur supports and inlay). The office itself existed from the late 10th century to King Chungseon's reign (1308-13), so the name alone allows a much wider span.
rows.what_it_tells: The box was made to hold medicine for the court's medical office; it is a court-commissioned item, and kiln finds tie the type to Yongun-ri, Gangjin.
rows.cautions: Two technique variants exist (inlaid and incised), so either is consistent with the type. The start date of the office differs between sources (990 vs. reign of Mokjong). None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: On the Handok Museum of Medicine box (Treasure 646) the characters 尙藥局 are inlaid in white on the side of the lid and of the lower body.
On the National Museum of Korea box (Treasure 1023) the same office name is incised, not inlaid, on the sides of lid and body where they meet.
Sangyakguk was the Goryeo government office in charge of medicine, so these boxes are read as medicine containers.

Sources differ on when the office began: the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (citing Goryeosa) says it already existed in 990 (Seongjong 9) and lasted to King Chungseon's reign, later renamed Bonguiseo (奉醫署) and Jeonuisi (典醫寺); the heritage record says from King Mokjong (r. 997-1009) to King Chungseon (r. 1308-13).
The inlaid box is dated to about the mid-12th century on the evidence of its glaze, quartz spur supports and inlay; the heritage record dates it to around the 12th century.

Celadon sherds bearing the same 尙藥局 inscription were excavated at the Yongun-ri kiln site, Daegu-myeon, Gangjin; similar boxes are held by the National Museum of Korea and the Museum Yamato Bunkakan, Japan.
facts.quote: 상약국명 청자 파편이 … 용운리 가마터에서 출토

facts.text: Yun Yong-i lists a covered bowl with incised cloud-and-dragon design inscribed Sangyakguk, and a lid with the same design inscribed Sangyakguk in white inlay, among 12th-century carved celadons.

rows.chars: 淳化四年癸巳太廟第一室享器匠崔吉會造
variants: 淳化四年 癸巳 太廟第一室 享器匠 崔吉會 造
rows.hangul: 순화사년 계사 태묘제일실 향기 장 최길회 조
rows.rr: Sunhwa sanyeon gyesa Taemyo jeilsil hyanggi jang Choe Gil-hoe jo
rows.mr: Sunhwa sanyŏn kyesa T'aemyo cheilsil hyanggi chang Ch'oe Kirhoe cho
rows.meaning: 'Fourth year of Chunhua [Song era name], gyesa year [993]: ritual vessel for the First Chamber of the Royal Ancestral Shrine; made by the craftsman Choe Gil-hoe'
wares: early celadon (some scholars: early white porcelain)
rows.technique: incised
rows.where_on_object: underside of the foot (base), running around it
rows.date_note: 淳化 (Chunhua) is a Northern Song era name; its 4th year, a gyesa year, is 993 = King Seongjong 12. The shrine (太廟) was begun in 989 and completed in 992, so the jar was made the year after completion.
rows.what_it_tells: The earliest firmly dated Goryeo ceramic: it shows that by 993 Goryeo kilns were making high-fired glazed wares for state ritual, and that Goryeo dated items with the Song era name. It names a ritual use (Taejo's chamber of the ancestral shrine) and a craftsman.
rows.cautions: A unique museum item (Ewha Womans University Museum, National Treasure). Sources call its ware either early celadon or early white porcelain. KHS glosses Choe Gil-hoe as 'craftsman (or supervisor)'. The parsing of 享器匠 is read as 享器 + 匠 by most sources. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The base of the jar is incised with 淳化四年癸巳 太廟第一室享器匠崔吉會造.
facts.quote: 淳化四年癸巳 太廟第一室享器匠崔吉會造

facts.text: Sunhwa (淳化) year 4 is 993, the 12th year of King Seongjong; it is the oldest known dated Goryeo ceramic (the earliest complete dated inscribed celadon).
facts.quote: 현재까지 알려진 가장 오래된 재명(在銘) 고려자기

facts.text: The Goryeo royal ancestral shrine (Taemyo) was begun in 989 and completed in 992, so the jar dates from the year after its completion; the First Chamber held King Taejo's spirit tablet.
The jar is thought to have been made at the Wonsan-ri kiln, Baecheon-gun, Hwanghae-do (now North Korea), by comparison with excavated sherds in quality and in the way inscriptions were cut.
facts.quote: 원산리 가마터에서 제작되어 태묘 제기로 사용된 것으로 추정

facts.text: A stem cup inscribed 淳化三年 (992) was excavated in 1989-90 by North Korea's Institute of Archaeology at Wonsan-ri kiln no. 2; Ewha's own label likewise reports a shard dated 992 from the Wonsan kiln.
facts.quote: 순화3년 명 고배(淳化三年‘銘 高杯)

facts.text: Its glaze is a grayish pale green that falls short of true celadon, and some scholars regard the jar as early white porcelain.
facts.quote: 이 항아리를 초기 백자로 보는 견해도 있다

facts.text: It was designated Treasure 237 in 1963 and raised to National Treasure in 2019 (designated 2019-05-02).
facts.quote: 보물 제237호 '청자 순화4년 명 항아리'를 국보로 지정 예고

facts.text: The heritage record describes Choe Gil-hoe as the craftsman or possibly the supervising official.

rows.meaning: Late-Goryeo inlaid celadon bearing a cyclical (sexagenary) year name; eight different years are recorded
wares: inlaid celadon (bowls, dishes, four-lug jars, cups, stem cups)
rows.technique: inlaid (black or white slip), on vessels whose decoration is often stamped and then inlaid
rows.where_on_object: usually the center of the interior bottom, often within a double circle
rows.date_note: The eight years fall either in 1269-1295 or in 1329-1355 (cycles beginning 1264 and 1324). Older scholarship (Nomori Ken; Choe Sun-u, Chung Yangmo, Choi Gun) put gisa-imo in the late 13th century; Yun Yong-i and others, and most recent work, put all eight in the early-mid 14th century. Jeonghae is agreed to be 1347.
rows.what_it_tells: A cyclical year inscribed on late-Goryeo inlaid celadon, usually from the Gangjin kilns, made as tribute ware. It narrows the date to one of two (or more) 60-year cycles; with style it is a key benchmark for 13th-14th century inlaid celadon.
rows.cautions: Never read a ganji as one fixed year: each recurs every 60 years. Museums still catalogue the same years differently (the V&A records its two gisa items as 1389, a third cycle, while its own summary says 1269/1329). 辛未, sometimes listed, does not appear in any list of known ganji celadons found. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: Eight cyclical years are known on celadon: 己巳 gisa, 庚午 gyeongo, 壬申 imsin, 癸酉 gyeyu, 甲戌 gapsul, 壬午 imo, 乙未 eulmi and 丁亥 jeonghae.
facts.quote: 정해(丁亥), 을미(乙未) 등 8종이 있다

facts.text: Ganji inscriptions are typically on the interior bottom of the vessel.
facts.quote: 그릇의 안쪽 바닥 중앙에 ‘己巳(기사)’ 명문

facts.text: A ganji does not give an exact year, because the same pair recurs every 60 years; the eight known pairs fall in 1269-1295 or 1329-1355.
facts.quote: does not provide the exact date

facts.text: Choe Sun-u, Chung Yangmo and Choi Gun dated the ganji celadons from gisa to imo to the late 13th century and jeonghae to the mid-14th; Yun Yong-i and Gao Yuxie (as transliterated in the translation; possibly 高裕燮 Ko Yu-seop) dated all eight to the early-mid 14th century.
Earlier attributions (e.g. imsin = 1272) followed Nomori Ken; the later cycle (1332) is now considered more likely.

Recent scholarship holds that all ganji celadons were made in the early-to-mid 14th century, avoiding the awkward gap the older dating implied between the 13th-century group and the 1347 jeonghae group.
facts.quote: 모든 간지명 청자가 14세기 전·중반 사이에 집중적으로 제작

facts.text: Jeon Seungchang compared ganji bowls with gold-painted celadon (recorded in Goryeosa in 1289 and 1297): the ganji items have simpler, later-looking scroll designs, so he places them in the early 14th century.
Ganji celadons were produced at Gangjin kilns Sadang-ri no. 7, Gyeyul-ri no. 18 and Sudong-ri no. 1; a ganji (imo) shard was also found at Yucheon-ri kiln no. 12, Buan.
facts.quote: 사당리 7호 요지와 계율리 18호 요지, 수동리 1호 요지

facts.text: They have been found at Manwoldae (Gaeseong palace), Unjusa, Jeseoksa and Seonwonsa; a gisa bowl and about 100 inlaid celadons were raised off Boryeong (Jukdo) in 1987.
Lee Jongmin interprets the ganji as a control mark on tribute ware, meant to raise quality and stop intermediaries embezzling Gangjin tribute celadon.
facts.quote: 간지명 청자는 공납 자기로 보아도 좋을 것이다

facts.text: The Gangjin kilns lie at Yongun-ri (mostly early Goryeo), Gyeyul-ri (early and late inlaid celadon), Sadang-ri (peak and late) and Sudong-ri (mostly late Goryeo), Daegu-myeon.
From the colonial period, the making, supply and sale of 'reproduction' Goryeo celadon (재현청자) were monopolised by Japanese residents in Korea; the abstract does not discuss copied inscriptions.
The standard catalogue is Haegang Ceramics Museum, 『고려시대 후기 간지명 상감청자』 (1991), with essays by Chung Yangmo and Yun Yong-i on the dating.

rows.meaning: Cyclical year Gisa: 1269 or 1329 (see ganjimyeong-sanggam-cheongja)
rows.technique: inlaid (black or white)
rows.date_note: 1269 (13th-century cycle) or 1329 (14th-century cycle). Recent scholarship favours 1329. The V&A catalogues its items to 1389 (the next cycle).
rows.what_it_tells: Late-Goryeo Gangjin-type inlaid celadon, probably tribute ware; date to one of two cycles.
rows.cautions: A ganji is not a single year; check which cycle a catalogue uses. Catalogue dates for 己巳 include 1269, 1329 and (V&A) 1389. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: 己巳 (Gisa) is one of the eight cyclical years recorded on late-Goryeo inlaid celadon.
As a sexagenary year 己巳 corresponds to 1269 or 1329 in the two cycles that scholars debate (1264- and 1324-cycles).
The 己巳 bowl from the Jukdo (Boryeong) underwater site has the inscription at the center of the interior bottom; it is read as about 1329 (Chungsuk 16), though some read 1269 (Wonjong 10).
Jeon Seungchang dates the Leeum gisa bowl (inlaid peony scroll) to 1329 rather than 1269 because its scroll band is simpler than on late-13th-century gold-painted celadon.
Lee Jongmin's 1994 article gave 1269 for an NMK gisa dish (noting it 'has also been dated 1329'); his later Uri Yeoksanet text captions a Haegang gisa bowl as 1329.

The V&A holds two gisa items (C.570-1918, 己巳 in black inlay; C.578-1918, in white inlay), attributed to a Sadang-ri kiln, Gangjin; its records give the production date as 1389 while the summary says 1269/1329.

As a sexagenary year 庚午 corresponds to 1270 or 1330 in the two cycles that scholars debate (1264- and 1324-cycles).
The Fitzwilliam Museum holds a bowl (C.76-1984) with 'kyongo' inlaid in its center (record seen only as a search snippet; site under maintenance).

facts.text: 壬申 (Imsin) is one of the eight cyclical years recorded on late-Goryeo inlaid celadon.
As a sexagenary year 壬申 corresponds to 1272 or 1332 in the two cycles that scholars debate (1264- and 1324-cycles).
Jeon Seungchang dates the Leeum stem cup with inlaid lotus scroll and imsin inscription to 1332 rather than 1272, because its lotus motif is looser than on the gold-painted vase.
The Fitzwilliam Museum dates its imsin bowl (C.77-1984) to 1332, noting earlier scholars followed Nomori Ken's 1272.

As a sexagenary year 癸酉 corresponds to 1273 or 1333 in the two cycles that scholars debate (1264- and 1324-cycles).

rows.meaning: Cyclical year Imo: 1282 or 1342 (see ganjimyeong-sanggam-cheongja)
rows.technique: inlaid (black or white)
rows.date_note: 1282 (13th-century cycle) or 1342 (14th-century cycle). Recent scholarship favours 1342.
rows.what_it_tells: Late-Goryeo Gangjin-type inlaid celadon, probably tribute ware; date to one of two cycles. The Yucheon-ri find shows ganji wares were also made at Buan, not only Gangjin.
rows.cautions: A ganji is not a single year; check which cycle a catalogue uses. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. facts.text: 壬午 (Imo) is one of the eight cyclical years recorded on late-Goryeo inlaid celadon.
As a sexagenary year 壬午 corresponds to 1282 or 1342 in the two cycles that scholars debate (1264- and 1324-cycles).
A celadon bowl shard inlaid in white with 壬午 at the interior bottom was excavated in 1966 at Yucheon-ri kiln 12 (Buan); Koo Illhoe reads it as probably 1342 rather than 1282 or 1402.
Lee Jongmin notes an NMK imo dish with chrysanthemum decoration that, unusually, has a trimmed foot ring (the translation's date figures for it are garbled).

rows.meaning: Cyclical year Eulmi: 1295 or 1355 (see ganjimyeong-sanggam-cheongja)
rows.technique: inlaid (black or white)
rows.date_note: 1295 (13th-century cycle) or 1355 (14th-century cycle). Recent scholarship favours 1355.
rows.what_it_tells: Late-Goryeo Gangjin-type inlaid celadon, probably tribute ware; date to one of two cycles.
rows.cautions: A ganji is not a single year; check which cycle a catalogue uses. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. facts.text: 乙未 (Eulmi) is one of the eight cyclical years recorded on late-Goryeo inlaid celadon.
As a sexagenary year 乙未 corresponds to 1295 or 1355 in the two cycles that scholars debate (1264- and 1324-cycles).
The Fitzwilliam Museum has a bowl fragment (C.584-1984) inlaid 'ulmi', dated probably 1355 (record seen only as a search snippet).

rows.meaning: Cyclical year jeonghae, agreed to be 1347
rows.technique: inlaid (black or white)
rows.date_note: Both camps date jeonghae to 1347 (it was found with a 至正 sherd). Lee Jongmin's Uri Yeoksanet text once writes 1345, an internal slip (至正 jeonghae = 1347).
rows.what_it_tells: Late-Goryeo Gangjin-type inlaid celadon, probably tribute ware; date to one of two cycles.
rows.cautions: Lee's Uri Yeoksanet page gives both 1345 and 1347 for the same group; 1347 is the arithmetic and the consensus. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: 丁亥 (Jeonghae) is one of the eight cyclical years recorded on late-Goryeo inlaid celadon.
As a sexagenary year 丁亥 corresponds to 1287 or 1347 in the two cycles that scholars debate (1264- and 1324-cycles).
A jeonghae sherd was found in the same layer as a 至正 (Yuan era 1341-67) sherd in the National Museum's 1960s excavation at Sadang-ri kiln no. 7, so jeonghae is dated to 1347.
facts.quote: 이를 근거로 정해명은 1347년경에 제작된 것이 밝혀졌다

facts.text: Jeonghae items are mostly small dishes, with thin yellowish-brown crackled glaze, roughly scraped bottoms and sand supports; a flower-shaped jeonghae dish came from the Unjusa temple site, Hwasun.
facts.quote: often appears in small plate types

rows.meaning: Zhizheng, Yuan-dynasty era name (1341-1368)
rows.technique: black inlay inside a double roundel
rows.where_on_object: center of the interior bottom of a small dish
rows.date_note: The era ran 1341-1367/68; Goryeosa records a ban on Yuan era names in 1356 (Gongmin 5), so if obeyed the item dates 1341-1356 (Lee 1994). Lee's later text gives 1341-1365.
rows.what_it_tells: A Yuan era name on Gangjin celadon: mid-14th century, under Yuan overlordship.
rows.cautions: Known from sherds (Haegang Ceramics Museum; NMK survey at Sadang-ri). Both descriptions found are by the same author (Lee Jongmin). None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: A sherd from Sadang-ri, Gangjin (Haegang Ceramics Museum) has 至正 inlaid in black inside a double roundel at the center, with ruyi-head decoration; a similar sherd came from the National Museum's Sadang-ri survey begun in 1963.
至正 is a Yuan era name (1341-1367); Goryeosa records that its use was banned after Gongmin 5 (1356), giving 1341-1356 if the ban was obeyed.
facts.quote: 공민왕 5년(1356)에는 원의 연호를 사용하지 못하도록 하교

rows.meaning: Jeongneung, the tomb of Princess Noguk (노국대장공주, d. 1365), consort of King Gongmin
rows.technique: white inlay (Lee 1994); bowls with stamped-and-inlaid lotus/peony scroll
rows.date_note: After Princess Noguk's death in 1365; the tomb was maintained until King Gongmin's death in 1374, so Jeon and Koo date the group 1365-1374.
rows.what_it_tells: Made for rites at a named royal tomb: a firm late-14th-century benchmark, and proof that Gangjin still supplied the court at the end of Goryeo.
rows.cautions: English sources name the queen differently (Lee: Princess Noguk Daejang; Koo: 'Queen Jangmok'; Jeon: Queen Indeok 仁德王后). Some 正陵 celadons first surfaced through Japanese looting of the tomb in 1905-1920. Similar uninscribed bowls are common in late-Goryeo and early-buncheong kilns. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The NMK large bowl has 正陵 inlaid in white on the interior bottom; Jeongneung was the tomb of Princess Noguk Daejang, King Gongmin's consort, who died in 1365, and the vessels were used for its funerary rites.
Scholars date Jeongneung-inscribed wares 1365-1374, since the tomb was maintained until King Gongmin's death in 1374.

A fragment with the same inscription was found at Sadang-ri, Gangjin, by a Japanese archaeologist in 1928 (Nomori Ken); ten such vessels survive, including finds from the Seonwonsa temple site, Ganghwa.
Jeongneung wares were thought to be made only at Gangjin, but shards with a very similar inlaid lotus scroll were excavated at Yucheon-ri, Buan, in 1966.
Japan looted the tomb thirteen times between 1905 and 1920, and inlaid celadon inscribed 正陵 became known through this looting.
facts.quote: 정릉(正陵)의 명문이 새겨진 상감청자가 도굴되어 알려지기도

rows.meaning: '[Year] euryu (also romanized eulyu, ulyu), Saonseo' - the court office for brewing wine for state rites
rows.technique: black inlay
rows.where_on_object: running from the shoulder down the body
rows.date_note: The office bore the name Saonseo in 1308-1355, 1362-1368 and from 1372 into early Joseon; the only eulyu year in those spans is 1345 (Lee 1994; the translation's 'first year of King Gongmin' should be King Chungmok's first year).
rows.what_it_tells: A wine bottle supplied to the court wine office; with 德泉 items it shows maebyeong were wine vessels.
rows.cautions: Lee's English translation names the wrong king for 1345. Office names straddle Goryeo and Joseon. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: An NMK maebyeong with willow decoration has 乙酉司醞署 in black inlay from shoulder to lower body; Saonseo brewed alcohol for state ceremonies.
facts.quote: from the shoulder to the lower body

facts.text: The office (founded as Yangonseo 良醞署 under Munjong) was called Saonseo in 1308-1355, 1362-1368 and 1372 into early Joseon; the eulyu year within these spans is 1345.
14th-century celadon maebyeong bearing office names such as 司醞署 or 德泉 show that the maebyeong was used as a wine vessel.
司醞署 is listed with 寶原庫, 德泉庫 and 義城庫 among office names on mid-to-late 14th-century celadon maebyeong.
facts.quote: 사온서(司醞署), 보원고(寶原庫), 덕천고(德泉庫)

rows.meaning: Deokcheon(-go), a royal storehouse office (1298-1403)
rows.technique: black inlay
rows.date_note: Bounded by the office's existence (1298-1403). The Horim maebyeong is 14th century; office-named maebyeong of this S-shaped type are mostly late 14th to early 15th century.
rows.what_it_tells: Made for a palace storehouse; shows the transition from late inlaid celadon to inlaid buncheong.
rows.cautions: The office survived into Joseon (to 1403), so 德泉 alone does not prove a Goryeo date; many 德泉 items exist. The buncheong research row may also cover 德泉庫. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The Horim Museum maebyeong (Treasure, 2006) has 德泉 inlaid in black on the upper body; 德泉庫 existed 1298-1403, so the item was made in that span.
There are many celadons inscribed 德泉, but few with a well-preserved three-dimensional form, design and glaze like the Horim bottle; it is dated to the 14th century.
The NMK holds a comparable maebyeong inscribed 德泉庫 (靑磁 象嵌柳蓮文 德泉庫銘 梅甁); both show the shift from late inlaid celadon to early inlaid buncheong.
Office names such as 德泉(庫) and 義成庫 appear on late celadon maebyeong; one source dates the group mostly late 14th to early 15th century, the other mid-to-late 14th century.

rows.meaning: Uiseonggo, a royal storehouse office
rows.technique: inlaid (as recorded for this group)
rows.date_note: One source puts office-named maebyeong in the mid-to-late 14th century, another mostly in the late 14th to early 15th century.
rows.what_it_tells: A maebyeong supplied to a royal storehouse at the end of Goryeo or start of Joseon.
rows.cautions: Sources print the office as 義成庫 (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture) and 義城庫 (Jeonbuk Ilbo); the form on the ware itself was not seen. No museum example located. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: Office inscriptions such as 德泉 and 義成庫 are recorded on maebyeong of this S-shaped type, mostly late 14th to early 15th century.
facts.quote: ‘덕천(德泉)’, ‘의성고(義成庫)’ 등의 관사(官司) 명문

facts.text: 義城庫 is listed among office names on mid-to-late 14th-century celadon maebyeong.
facts.quote: 의성고(義城庫) 등의 관사명(官司名)

rows.meaning: Bowongo, a royal storehouse office
rows.technique: inlaid (as recorded for this group)
rows.date_note: Mid-to-late 14th century according to the one source.
rows.what_it_tells: A maebyeong supplied to a royal storehouse in the late 14th century.
rows.cautions: Single source (a newspaper report quoting the Buan museum's designation report); hanja printed 寶原庫. No item, image or kiln find located. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: 寶原庫 is named among office names on mid-to-late 14th-century celadon maebyeong.

rows.meaning: Jeongsasaek, a royal inner-palace office that prepared the king's Taoist rites
rows.technique: black inlay, in large characters
rows.date_note: The office is attested in Goryeosa from 1258 (Gojong 45) and abolished in 1391 (Gongyang 3); the vase's form and decoration place it in the later 14th century.
rows.what_it_tells: The only known ware naming this office: royal Taoist ritual use, late 14th century.
rows.cautions: Unique; no 淨事色 sherd has been found at a kiln site. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The Buan County Celadon Museum maebyeong (Jeonbuk Tangible Cultural Heritage 284, 2021) has 淨事色 inlaid in black in large characters at the center of the body, with willow and reed decoration.
It is the only known ware inscribed with the Goryeosa office name 淨事色 and none has been found at a kiln site; it is dated to the later 14th century.
Per the Goryeosa treatise on officials, 淨事色 first appears in 1258 and was abolished in 1391; it prepared the king's Taoist rites.

rows.meaning: Saseonseo, the office for royal court cuisine (1372-1432)
rows.technique: inlaid
rows.date_note: The office existed 1372-1432, spanning the last Goryeo decades and early Joseon; a news report places 司膳署 wares in the early 15th century.
rows.what_it_tells: Tableware for the royal kitchen at the Goryeo-Joseon transition, with very simplified scroll bands.
rows.cautions: May be early Joseon rather than Goryeo; overlaps the buncheong topic. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: A Leeum bowl with inlaid scroll design is inscribed 司膳, referring to Saseonseo, the office for royal court cuisine, which lasted from 1372 to 1432.
司膳署 is listed among office names on early-15th-century celadon.

rows.meaning: Yeollyesaek ('Banquet-Rites Office'; Lee's translation spells it Yeonryesaek)
rows.technique: inlaid
rows.date_note: Dated to the 14th century by its clay and design technique.
rows.what_it_tells: A dish for a court banquet office, of a new 14th-century shape that buncheong later continued.
rows.cautions: Single source; the office's dates were not found. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: A dish with crane-and-cloud design is inscribed 宴禮色; it is dated to the 14th century and its outward-rim shape links to Yuan Jingdezhen wares and to later stamped buncheong.

rows.meaning: 'Burning [paper] money' - the Taoist ritual; 燒錢色 is the office that conducted it
rows.technique: painted, incised or inlaid
rows.date_note: Kim Yunjeong dates the NMK cups to the late 13th century; Park Jiyoung, from the Gaeseong palace excavations, argues they were used in the first half of the 13th century.
rows.what_it_tells: Altar cups for royal Taoist rites (choje) held by the Sojeonsaek office.
rows.cautions: Date disputed (first vs. second half of the 13th century). None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: More than ten Goryeo celadons are known with painted, incised or inlaid 燒錢 or 燒錢色; most are cups, read as altar cups for Taoist choje rites.
Goryeosa (1278) records that 燒錢色 requested wine for rites, and the Taejo sillok (1392) lists 燒錢色 among Goryeo Taoist ritual places to be abolished.
Park Jiyoung redates the 燒錢 celadons from the late to the first half of the 13th century, using associated ○/⊙ and 成 marks and their find-spot behind Seongyeongjeon Hall at the palace.

rows.rr: Chirwon jeonbae / Sibiryo jeonbae / Cheonhwang jeonbae
rows.mr: Ch'irwŏn chŏnbae / Sibiryo chŏnbae / Ch'ŏnhwang chŏnbae
rows.meaning: 'Front row before the Seven Primordials (Northern Dipper)', '...before the Eleven Luminaries', '...before the Heavenly Emperor': places on a Taoist altar
rows.technique: inlaid (black on the bottle, one character on each of four sides)
rows.where_on_object: dishes: not specified; bottle: four sides of the body
rows.date_note: Dated to the late 13th century by Kim Yunjeong.
rows.what_it_tells: Vessels set before named star deities in royal Taoist choje rites.
rows.cautions: Single source. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: Celadon dishes inscribed 七元前排 and 十一曜前排 (NMK) and a bottle inscribed 天皇前排 (Gangjin Celadon Museum) were ritual wares placed before the named deities in choje; the bottle has one character in black inlay on each of four sides.
facts.quote: 七元前排, 十一曜前排, 天皇前排

rows.meaning: The Three Officials (of Heaven, Earth and Water), Taoist deities
rows.technique: inlaid
rows.date_note: Late 13th century (Kim Yunjeong).
rows.what_it_tells: A Taoist offering cup.
rows.cautions: Single source for the inscription. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: A Gangjin Celadon Museum cup is inlaid 三官, the Taoist officials of heaven, earth and water.
The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture reads 王-inscribed cup stands as vessels for offering tea or wine to the Taoist Heaven, Earth and Water Officials.
facts.quote: 천관 · 지관 · 수관과 같은 도교상에 차나 술을 올리기

rows.meaning: 'Heaven', 'Earth', 'Ghosts' - single characters on Taoist ritual dishes and cups
rows.technique: inlaid
rows.date_note: Late 13th to early 14th century (Kim Yunjeong's figure dates).
rows.what_it_tells: High-quality (silica-supported) ritual vessels for Samgyecho or festival rites.
rows.cautions: Single source; single characters are easy to confuse with other marks. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: Celadon dishes and cups inlaid with 天, 地 or 鬼 are otherwise undecorated, fired on silica supports, and are thought to have served Taoist rites (Samgyecho or the Sangwon/Jungwon festivals).
facts.quote: cheon (天, heaven) or ji (地, earth)

rows.meaning: 'King' (royal)
wares: inlaid celadon cups and cup stands
rows.technique: black inlay
rows.where_on_object: inner side of the flaring petals of a cup stand
rows.date_note: Estimated late 13th century, when royal Taoist rites were frequent (late 13th to early 14th century).
rows.what_it_tells: A royal ritual vessel from the Gangjin (Sadang-ri) kilns, probably for offering tea or wine in Taoist rites.
rows.cautions: The encyclopedia entry cites the heritage portal, so the two sources are not fully independent. 王 is a common character; on other wares it can mean other things. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The Gangjin Goryeo Celadon Museum cup stand (Jeonnam Tangible Cultural Heritage, 2008) has 王 in black inlay on the petal-shaped flange.
facts.quote: ‘王’명(銘)이 흑상감되어 있는 매우 양질의 청자

facts.text: 王-inscribed celadons survive mainly as cups and cup stands, suggesting ritual rather than everyday use; they are thought to have been made for 13th-century royal Taoist rites.
王 sherds are collected at Sadang-ri kilns 7 and 41, Gangjin, so production is placed at Sadang-ri; the cup stand itself was recovered around kiln 41.

rows.meaning: 'Completed / made' - read as a workshop mark; meaning still uncertain
wares: celadon tableware (bowls, dishes, cups, covered bowls, bottles)
rows.technique: brushed in underglaze iron (Sadang-ri 7 group); other forms not specified
rows.where_on_object: center of the inside of the foot (base)
rows.date_note: Han Seong-uk dates the iron-brushed 成 group to the second quarter of the 13th century; Koo Illhoe says production ran at least into the first half of the 13th century.
rows.what_it_tells: Good but not top-grade Gangjin/Buan tableware of the early-mid 13th century, for users below the royal family.
rows.cautions: Sources disagree on spread: Han says the iron-brushed 成 comes only from Sadang-ri 7; Koo says 成-inscribed celadon came from about 100 kilns in Gangjin and Buan. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: Underglaze-iron 成 celadons are brushed at the center of the inner foot and are found only at Sadang-ri kiln 7; varied handwriting suggests a workshop rather than one potter.
facts.quote: 굽안바닥 중앙에 명문(銘文)을 쓰고 있다

facts.text: Celadons inscribed 成 were found around Sadang-ri kiln 7 with high-grade wares inscribed 御件; the reason for and meaning of the inscription are unknown.
Han dates the 成 group to the second quarter of the 13th century, as wares for a rank below the royal family and high aristocracy.
Koo reports 成-inscribed celadon from about 100 kilns, including Yongun-ri, Gyeyul-ri and Sadang-ri (Gangjin) and some 70 kilns at Yucheon-ri, Jinseo-ri and elsewhere in Buan.
成 celadons occur among the inscribed wares from the Gaeseong palace site and help date the 燒錢 cups.

rows.meaning: Incised circle and circle-with-dot marks
wares: press-molded celadon (bowls, dishes, cups, bottles, boxes)
rows.technique: incised
rows.where_on_object: center of the inside of the foot (base)
rows.date_note: Second quarter of the 13th century, centered on the 1230s, from finds at King Huijong's tomb (Seongneung), Hyeeumwon and Kamakura.
rows.what_it_tells: High-quality Gangjin (Sadang-ri) celadon of the 1230s, found at elite and government sites.
rows.cautions: Interpretations differ: a workshop mark (Han) or a marker for the tax-transport and distribution system (Jang). None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The ○ and ⊙ marks are incised at the center of the inner base; they came from Sadang-ri kilns 8, 23 and 27, ⊙ only from 23 and 27.
facts.quote: 굽안바닥 중앙에 부호를 새긴 것으로 제작자(공방)를 표기

facts.text: Han dates them to the second quarter of the 13th century (1230s) and reads them as workshop marks.
Jang Namwon lists the marked wares from Sadang-ri kilns 8, 10, 23, 27 and 38 and suggests the marks served the tax-transport and central-storage distribution system.
facts.quote: used as a kind of marker

rows.meaning: 'Item for royal use' (vessels for court use)
rows.technique: not specified
rows.date_note: No date given; found with the 成 group near Sadang-ri kiln 7 (13th century context).
rows.what_it_tells: Made for the king or court at Sadang-ri, Gangjin.
rows.cautions: Single source; no item described. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: High-quality celadons inscribed 御件 ('vessels for court use') were found around Sadang-ri kiln 7, Gangjin.
facts.quote: eogeon (御件, vessels for court use)

rows.meaning: Hyomun, a potter's name
rows.technique: written on the foot (technique not specified)
rows.where_on_object: one corner of the foot base
rows.date_note: The Leeum maebyeong is dated to the later 12th century.
rows.what_it_tells: A named potter whose name also appears on Yucheon-ri finds, so the item is attributed to the Buan kilns.
rows.cautions: Both statements come from the national heritage agency (two records); no independent scholarly source was read. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The Leeum maebyeong with incised lotus (National Treasure 252) has the maker's name 孝文 written on one corner of the foot base, which shows it was made at the Yucheon-ri kilns, Buan.
facts.quote: 굽바닥 한 모서리에 ‘효문(孝文)’이라는 만든 사람의 이름

facts.text: The characters 孝文 and 照淸 occur on finds from the Yucheon-ri kiln site.

rows.meaning: Literally 'Hyogu carved [it]' - a carver's/potter's signature (reading of 刻 as 'carved' is literal)
rows.technique: not specified
rows.date_note: Grouped by Yun Yong-i with 12th-century carved celadons.
rows.what_it_tells: A rare carver's or potter's signature on 12th-century carved celadon.
rows.cautions: Single source; item in the Nezu Museum, Tokyo. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: A wine bottle with incised lotus vinescroll in the Nezu Museum bears the inscription 孝久刻.

rows.meaning: Jocheong, presumed to be a Buddhist monk's name
rows.technique: not specified
rows.date_note: Bounded by the main activity of the Yucheon-ri kilns (mid-12th to first half of 13th century).
rows.what_it_tells: Buan wares often name temples (Hwanghasa, Cheongnimsa) or monks (Uijang, Donjin, Donjang, Eungji, Jocheong), showing a close Buddhist clientele.
rows.cautions: The hanja for the other Buan temple and monk names were not found. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: 照淸 (Jocheong) is recorded on Buan (Yucheon-ri) celadon finds: the heritage record gives the characters, and Jeon Seungchang lists Jocheong among presumed monks' names on Buan relics.
Buan kiln finds are often inscribed with temple names (Hwanghasa, Cheongnimsa) or presumed monks' names (Uijang, Donjin, Donjang, Eungji, Jocheong).

rows.meaning: 'Poem'
rows.technique: white inlay
rows.date_note: Listed by Yun Yong-i among celadons he dates 1170-1180.
rows.what_it_tells: An early use of inlay to add a word to a carved item.
rows.cautions: Single source (NMK item). None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: An NMK gourd-shaped bottle with incised lotus vinescroll bears the character 詩 in white inlay.
facts.quote: inscription si 詩 in white inlay

rows.meaning: 'Bring in the Wine' - title of a poem by the Tang poet Li He (790-816), inlaid with its full text
rows.technique: black inlay (title); poem text in four tablet-shaped panels
rows.where_on_object: title among willow branches; poem in four panels around the body
rows.date_note: Catalogued as late Goryeo to early Joseon.
rows.what_it_tells: A rare poem-inscribed wine bottle; Chinese drinking poetry on a Korean wine vessel.
rows.cautions: Single source; do not 'correct' the inlaid text to the standard Li He text. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The Leeum maebyeong (Treasure 1389) has the title 將進酒 inlaid in black among willow branches and the poem, by Li He, inlaid in four tablet-shaped panels; it is dated late Goryeo to early Joseon.

rows.meaning: Sanskrit (Siddham) mantra syllables, often in a concentric 'wheel' (字輪) arrangement
rows.technique: inlaid
rows.where_on_object: concentric rings (wheel mantra); single syllables on some sherds
rows.date_note: 13th-14th century; concentric-mantra items late 13th to early 14th century.
rows.what_it_tells: Esoteric Buddhist ritual ware (breaking hell, rebirth in the Pure Land), perhaps for rites for the dead, from a royal-ware kiln (Sadang-ri 23).
rows.cautions: Single scholarly source; single syllables could not be deciphered. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: Inlaid Sanskrit on celadon from Sadang-ri kiln 23 spells mantras in Siddham script, including the Six-Syllable Mantra and the Sweet Dew Mantra, often as concentric wheels; dated 13th-14th century.

rows.chars: 辛丑五月十日造 爲大口前戶正徐敢夫 / 淸沙硯壹雙黃河寺
variants: 辛丑五月十日造 爲大口前戶正徐取
rows.rr: Sinchuk owol sibil jo, wi Daegu jeon hojeong Seo Gam-bu / cheongsayeon ilssang Hwanghasa
rows.mr: Sinch'uk owŏl sibil cho, wi Taegu chŏn hojŏng Sŏ Kambu / ch'ŏngsayŏn ilssang Hwanghasa
rows.meaning: 'Made on the 10th day of the 5th month, sinchuk year, for Seo Gam-bu, former hojeong of Daegu' / 'clear-sand inkstones, one pair, Hwangha Temple'
rows.technique: white inlay (heritage record)
rows.where_on_object: underside (inside the foot / broad inner bottom), in three lines (24 characters per Jang)
rows.date_note: 辛丑 can be 1121, 1181 or 1241. The heritage record and Yun (1992) prefer 1181 (glaze and inlay); Jang Namwon (2008) and Yun (2004) put it at 1241.
rows.what_it_tells: A dated, dedicated inkstone naming a recipient from Daegu (大口, the Gangjin kiln district) and a temple; an anchor for dating inlaid celadon.
rows.cautions: Date and some characters are disputed (敢/取, 河/何, 壹 read 대 in the KHS hangul). Unique item (Leeum). None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: The underside of the Leeum inkstone (Treasure 1382) is inlaid in white with 辛丑五月十日造 爲大口前戶正徐敢夫 on the right and 淸沙硯壹雙黃河寺 on the left.
Yun Yong-i (1992) reads the second line's name as 徐取(?)夫 and the temple as 黃何寺.
facts.quote: 爲大口前戶正徐取(?) 夫

facts.text: The heritage record notes 辛丑 could be 1121, 1181 or 1241 and judges 1181 most likely from the glaze and inlay; Yun (1992) also gives 1181.
Jang Namwon dates the inkstone probably to 1241 and suggests it was a gift in gratitude to an office in Gangjin; Yun's 2004 article likewise gives 1241.

rows.rr: Gichuk guwol il / Gyeongin / Gyechungnyeon josang daeseong jibal / Sinyu
rows.mr: Kich'uk kuwŏl il / Kyŏngin / Kyech'ungnyŏn chosang taesŏng chibal / Sinyu
rows.meaning: Cyclical-year dates on 11th-13th-century celadons: 'gichuk year, 9th month, [blank] day'; 'gyeongin'; 'made in the gyechuk year ... alms bowl of the Great Sage'; 'sinyu'
rows.technique: relief (己丑); underglaze iron (庚寅); inlaid (癸丑); not stated (辛酉)
rows.date_note: Each pair has several possible cycles and authors have moved them: 己丑 1049 / 1109 / 1229; 庚寅 1110 / 1170 / 1230; 癸丑 1073 / 1193 / 1253; 辛酉 1141 (item known only from a photograph).
rows.what_it_tells: Rare dated items used to build the 12th-13th-century chronology; their absolute dates are not settled.
rows.cautions: All dates here come from one author (Yun Yong-i, 1992 and 2004), who revised his own dates by 60-120 years, citing Choe Sun-u's 1963-64 articles. Treat any single year as provisional. None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: A Ho-Am (Leeum) wide-mouthed celadon bottle carries 己丑九月日 in relief; Yun (1992) dated it 1109, and in 2004 to 1229, noting Choe Sun-u's first reading of 1049.
An NMK inlaid alms bowl is inscribed 癸丑年造上 大聖持鉢; once dated 1073, Yun moved it to 1193 (1992) and later 1253 (2004).
facts.quote: 癸丑年造上 大聖持鉢

facts.text: A maebyeong with a gyeongin date written in iron under the glaze, once dated 1110, was placed by Yun in 1170 (1992) and later 1230 (2004); the 1992 translation also misprints it 'gyeongjin'.
An iron-painted celadon ewer inscribed 辛酉 (dated 1141) survives only as a photograph.
facts.quote: remains to us only as a photograph

rows.meaning: 'Daepyeong' - meaning not explained in the record found
wares: celadon roof tile (curved tile with relief pomegranate-flower design)
rows.technique: not specified
rows.date_note: Goryeo; the record says date and purpose are established but does not state them.
rows.what_it_tells: The only complete inscribed celadon roof tile; Gangjin made celadon tiles for buildings.
rows.cautions: Single source; reading and meaning of 大平 not established here (do not assume an era name). None of the sources consulted mention later copies carrying this inscription; that is not evidence that none exist. Goryeo-style celadon has been reproduced since the colonial period, so the inscription alone does not by itself date the item or show that it is genuine.

facts.text: A Gangjin celadon curved roof tile with relief pomegranate-flower design inscribed 大平 (Jeonnam Tangible Cultural Heritage 388, 2024) is the only complete celadon tile with an inscription.

rows.hangul: 장흥고 세 글자를 새김 / 각 관사의 사호를 새김
rows.meaning: The 1417 order: tribute ware to be marked with the receiving office’s name (司號).
rows.technique: cut/stamped into the clay before firing (刻)
rows.date_note: Order dated 太宗 17年 4月 20日 (1417). Office-name and place-name marks on buncheong are dated from this point by Korean museums and scholars.
rows.what_it_tells: Explains why an office name appears on 15th-century buncheong: the ware was provincial tax/tribute ware for a named office in Seoul, and the mark was an anti-theft and accounting device.
rows.cautions: An inscription names the receiving office; it does not by itself date or proves genuine an item. A few office marks (義成庫, 恭安) belong to offices that predate or straddle 1417, so office marks were not invented in 1417.

facts.text: A Board of Revenue (戶曹) memorial of 1417 ordered that ceramic and wooden vessels owed as tribute to the Changhŭnggo be cut with its three-character name, and those for other offices with their own office names.
facts.quote: 今後刻長興庫三字…各刻司號

facts.text: Reason given: tribute ware passing through the Changhŭnggo to the kitchens was hidden or broken; the memorial asked that anyone found privately keeping a marked vessel be punished as for stealing government property. The king approved.
facts.quote: 有標器皿, 私藏現露者, 以盜官物坐罪

facts.text: The memorial names the offices that were to receive tribute ware directly: 司饔房, 司膳署, 禮賓, 典祀, 內資, 內贍寺, 恭安 and 敬承府.
facts.quote: 司饔房、司膳署、禮賓、典祀、內資、內贍寺、恭安、敬承府

facts.text: Korean museum and municipal texts state that office (官司名) and place (地名) inscriptions appear on buncheong from 1417.
facts.quote: 태종 17년(1417) 이후, 관아명(官衙銘)을 넣기 시작

facts.text: Place name + office name together record the producing county and the receiving office; the National Palace Museum describes the place as 제작지 (where made) and the office as 납품처 (where delivered).
In 1467 the Saongwŏn began running the Gwangju (Gyeonggi) kilns as the official court kiln; afterwards the provincial 磁器所 increasingly made ware for local needs rather than for central offices.
In 1466 the court restricted white porcelain to royal (進上) use; before that, white porcelain marked 內資, 內贍, 禮賓 was also supplied to offices.
facts.quote: 白磁器 除進上及已前燔造者外 自今公私 毋得用之

facts.text: Later rules: the Gyeongguk daejeon (1485) fixes 380 沙器匠 under the Saongwŏn but contains no inscription clause that we found.

Buncheong declined in the 16th century as slip-dipped and brushed wares turned into white porcelain; the encyclopedia names the Imjin War (1592–98) and changes in the ceramic-supply system as the end; the Gimhae city table ends its decline phase c.1510.

variants: 器皿底 書造作匠名
rows.hangul: 그릇 밑에 만든 장인의 이름을 씀
rows.meaning: The 1421 order: the maker’s name to be written on the base of vessels supplied to the court.
rows.technique: written/incised on the base
rows.date_note: Order dated 世宗 3年 4月 16日 (1421).
rows.what_it_tells: Explains short personal names incised inside the foot of some good-quality stamped buncheong: they identify the potter responsible for quality.
rows.cautions: Very few buncheong carry names; most kiln-site name marks are short and ambiguous (a surname alone such as 金).

facts.text: The Board of Works (工曹) complained that vessels for the court were carelessly made and broke soon; from now on the maker’s name was to be written on the base so that careless makers could be made to replace the vessels. Approved.
facts.quote: 於器皿底, 書造作匠名, 以憑後考

facts.text: NMK catalogue texts explain potters’ and production-place names on buncheong as a way to hold makers responsible for quality.
facts.quote: 도공이나 생산지의 이름을 새긴 것은 그릇 품질에 대한 책임

facts.text: At the Chunghyo-dong kiln (Gwangju) names such as 金, 朴金, 李万, 金咸, 朴用, 德金 are incised inside the foot of good-quality stamped wares and are read as craftsmen’s names.

rows.meaning: Changhŭnggo, the government storehouse that supplied mats, oiled paper and paper; by the 1417 order it also received tribute ceramic and wooden ware.
rows.technique: mostly stamped (印花) and white-inlaid; a few incised
rows.where_on_object: exterior wall, interior center, or one character per roundel; a place name is often on the opposite face
rows.date_note: 1417 order made 長興庫 compulsory on its tribute ware. The office itself ran 1392–1894, so it does not close the range; the stamped-ware style (15th c.) and any place name do.
rows.what_it_tells: Provincial tax ware made for the Changhŭnggo in Seoul, 15th century; with a place name it names the sending county, nearly always in Gyeongsang.
rows.cautions: Short form 長興 is also a Jeolla place name (長興); read it as the office only when paired (e.g. 義興長興, 善山長興). NMK titles two dishes oddly: 신수 7402 ‘수라장흥고’ with hanja 義羅長興, and 신수 1790 ‘부산 장흥고’ with hanja 金山仁興 — readings unresolved. No source found on modern copies.

facts.text: A Board of Revenue (戶曹) memorial of 1417 ordered that ceramic and wooden vessels owed as tribute to the Changhŭnggo be cut with its three-character name, and those for other offices with their own office names.
facts.quote: 今後刻長興庫三字…各刻司號

facts.text: The Changhŭnggo was created in 1308 (Goryeo), re-established in 1392 and handled cloth, paper and mats (in the Gyeongguk daejeon: mats, oiled paper, paper); it moved to the Royal Household Ministry in 1894.
Changhŭnggo marks occur with Gyeongsang place names: 慶州, 密陽, 梁山, 蔚山, 星州, 慶山, 陜川, 金山, 軍威, 淸道, 昌原, 咸安, 永川, 仁同, 順興, 義興, 善山, 金海.
Suffixes seen: 納 (‘delivered’) in 金山長興庫納 and 順興長興庫納; 執用 (‘for use by’) in 金海長興執用; 長興庫用 on a colonial-era NMK glass plate.
A 長興庫 bowl was excavated together with an epitaph dated 正統三年 (1438), a fixed point for Sejong-period stamped decoration.
Sherds inscribed 長興庫 were excavated at the Jangdae-ri kiln, Hapcheon.

rows.meaning: Naesŏmsi, the office supplying the palaces (especially the queen’s side), wine for senior officials and food for Japanese and Jurchen visitors.
rows.technique: stamped and white-inlaid; full form 內贍寺 also stamped
rows.where_on_object: usually interior center; sometimes exterior wall
rows.date_note: Office named Naesŏmsi from 1403 (formerly 德泉庫); marking ordered 1417. The office lasted to 1882 (merged with 義盈庫 1800 per sillokwiki; Namgaram gives 1403–1800).
rows.what_it_tells: Tribute ware for the Naesŏmsi, 15th century; the most common office mark at Seoul consumption sites, and made in many provinces including Jeolla.
rows.cautions: 內贍 also occurs on early white porcelain. Catalogue slips: NMK 개성 118 is dated ‘Goryeo’; Gangjin 고려청자 11781 is titled 內贍 but described as 司饔.

facts.text: 德泉庫 (founded 1392) was renamed Naesŏmsi in 1403 and put under the Board of Revenue in 1405; it supplied the palaces and senior officials and fed Japanese and Jurchen envoys; abolished 1882.
內贍寺 is one of the recipient offices named in the 1417 order.
At the Cheongjin 12–16 site in central Seoul, 34 early-Joseon items marked 內贍 were all buncheong, against three marked 內資.
Production evidence: 茂珍內贍 at the Chunghyo-dong kiln, Gwangju; 內贍 sherds at Boseong Jeongheung-ri, at the Imsil and Yeonggwang kilns, at Gangjin, at Wanju, and 內贍寺 sherds at Hakbong-ri, Gongju.
Bowls with 內贍 in the interior center were recovered from the seabed off Mado, Taean, showing that the ware was shipped by sea.
One NMK dish carries both 內贍 and 仁壽 (동원 789).

rows.meaning: Naejasi, the office supplying the royal household with rice, flour, wine, soy, oil, honey, vegetables and fruit, court banquets and weaving.
rows.technique: mostly stamped (印刻); the homophone 內子 is hand-incised (筆刻)
rows.date_note: Naejasi from 1401 (renamed from 內府寺), absorbed 義成庫 1403, abolished 1882; marks follow the 1417 order.
rows.what_it_tells: Tribute ware for the Naejasi; rarer than 內贍 because the king’s side also used silver, brass and white porcelain.
rows.cautions: 內子 is a same-sound miswriting of 內資, not a different office (and not ‘queen’).

facts.text: 內府寺 was renamed Naejasi in 1401 and took over the 義成庫 in 1403; the Gyeongguk daejeon defines its duties as royal provisions, banquets and weaving.
facts.quote: 掌內供米糆酒醬油蜜蔬果內宴織造

facts.text: 內資 is a recipient office in the 1417 order.
內子 on the NMK bowl 본관 13808 (綾城內子) and on sherds from Seoul sites is a homophone error for 內資; such items still circulated as Naejasi property.
facts.quote: 內子는 內資의 誤字

facts.text: 內資 buncheong was found in small numbers at kilns in Daejeon, Gongju and Gochang alongside 內贍 and 禮賓 wares.
The full form 內資寺 appears on a sherd photographed on an NMK colonial-era glass plate (건판 12098).

rows.meaning: Yebinsi, the office that entertained foreign envoys and served state banquets.
rows.technique: stamped and white-inlaid; also inlaid
rows.date_note: Office from 1392 (Goryeo origin) through the Joseon period; marks follow the 1417 order.
rows.what_it_tells: Tribute ware for the envoy-banquet office, 15th century; made in Chungcheong and Jeolla as well as Gyeongsang.
rows.cautions: 禮 is often written 礼 on the ware. A lone 礼 or 賓 is a fragmentary or abbreviated mark.

facts.text: The Yebinsi, re-established in 1392 from the Goryeo office, handled envoy reception and state banquets; it absorbed 義順庫 in 1403.
禮賓 is a recipient office in the 1417 order.
禮賓執用 (‘for the use of the Yebinsi’) occurs on NMK dishes.
A Mado (Taean seabed) dish reads 礼賓 made of four 礼 stamps and one 賓; a 礼 sherd near Undae-ri kiln 7, Goheung, is read as the office name.
Kiln and site finds: 禮賓 dishes and sherds from Hakbong-ri (Gongju), Cheongju and Jeonju collections.
Before 1466, white porcelain marked 礼賓 was also supplied to the office (five items at Cheongjin 1 site, Seoul).

rows.meaning: Insubu, household office first of Crown Prince Yi Bang-won (1400), then of the retired King Taejong (from 1418), later a royal storehouse.
rows.technique: stamped and white-inlaid
rows.where_on_object: often 仁, 壽, 府 in separate roundels on the exterior with the place name in the interior center
rows.date_note: Existed 1400.2–1400.11 (before marking began), then 1418.8–1455 (윤6월) and 1457.6 until abolished; sillok of 1465.2.22 says it was already abolished (NMK: 1464). Wares therefore c.1418–1455 or 1457–1465.
rows.what_it_tells: Tribute ware for the Insubu, mostly from Gyeongsang counties; the office dates bracket the item to 1418–1465.
rows.cautions: DISPUTED end date: NMK 동원 29 and Busan Museum texts say the office lasted to 1556; Namgaram says it lasted only Feb–Nov 1400; the sillok shows it abolished by 1465. 仁守 is a homophone error for 仁壽. NMK 신수 10978 is titled ‘영산이수부’, a slip for 仁壽府.

facts.text: Set up 1400.2.4 for Crown Prince Bang-won and abolished at his accession; restored 1418.8 when the crown-prince office 順承府 was renamed Insubu for the retired Taejong; kept after 1422 as a royal storehouse; renamed 德寧府 1455 and back to Insubu 1457; abolished in the 1460s.
A Board of Revenue entry of 1465.2.22 states the Insubu had already been abolished.

Kiln sites yielding Insubu sherds: Yangsan Gasan-ri, Changnyeong Cheongam-ri, Hapcheon Oesa-ri and Jangdae-ri, Goryeong Sabu-ri, Chilgok Haksang-ri, Gijang Jangan-ri, Sejong Geumsa-ri, Ulju Hajam-ri and Taegi-ri, Yeongam Sangwol-ri, Boryeong Pyeongna-ri, Yeongdong Sabu-ri.
The homophone 仁守 was excavated at the Sejong-ro site, Seoul.
Place combinations attested: 昌寧, 彦陽, 軍威, 三嘉/三加, 永川, 靈山, 蔚山, 慶山, 金山, 鎭海, 宜寧, 咸安, 善山.

rows.meaning: Kong’anbu, the household office of the retired King Jeongjong.
rows.technique: stamped; also black-and-white inlaid (恭安 bowl)
rows.date_note: Office 1400.11–1420.3; named among recipients in the 1417 order, so most marked items are probably 1417–1420.
rows.what_it_tells: A very early marked buncheong (before 1420) and a key fixed point for the first stamped and inlaid buncheong.

facts.text: Set up in 1400.11 when Jeongjong abdicated; abolished and merged into 仁寧府 in 1420.3.
恭安 is a recipient office in the 1417 order.
Bowls marked 恭安/恭安府 (with 敬承府) are cited as the dating evidence for the rise of stamped and inlaid buncheong; one is black-and-white inlaid with lotus scroll.
NMK holds a stamped bowl marked 恭安 (신수 1788).

rows.meaning: Kyŏngsŭngbu, the household office of Crown Prince Yangnyeong.
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Office 1402–1418; a 2018 study limits production of the marked items to April 1417–June 1418.
rows.what_it_tells: One of the earliest datable marked buncheong; four items are known.

facts.text: The Kyŏngsŭngbu was the crown prince’s office from 1402 to 1418.
敬承府 is a recipient office in the 1417 order.
Failed-firing 敬承府 sherds were found in the Jangdae-ri kiln dump (Hapcheon); four extant items are attributed there and dated April 1417–June 1418.

rows.meaning: Tŏngnyŏngbu, the household office of the retired King Danjong.
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Insubu renamed 德寧府 1455 (윤6월 12일) and renamed back 1457 (6월 25일).
rows.what_it_tells: A two-year window, so a dating reference for mature stamped buncheong.

facts.text: Renamed from Insubu in 1455 to serve the retired Danjong and changed back in 1457.
The encyclopedia cites the 德寧府 bowl among Sejo-period items showing the most refined stamped decoration.

rows.meaning: Sasŏnsŏ, the office that prepared the king’s meals.
rows.technique: stamped; also inlaid (jar with lotus and willow)
rows.date_note: Office 1392–1466 (renamed 司膳寺 1466, merged into 司饔院 1467.4).
rows.what_it_tells: Tribute ware for the royal kitchen office; made before 1467.

facts.text: Set up in 1392; renamed Sasŏnsi in 1466 and merged into the Saongwŏn in 1467.
司膳署 is a recipient office in the 1417 order and is among offices attested on buncheong.
司膳 sherds were excavated at the Jangdae-ri kiln; NMK holds an inlaid jar and a stamped bowl marked 司膳.

rows.meaning: Ŭisŏnggo, a royal storehouse inherited from Goryeo.
rows.technique: incised (vertically on the body)
rows.date_note: Merged into 內資寺 in 1403.6, so a 義成庫 item predates 1403 (and the 1417 order).
rows.what_it_tells: An office mark from before the 1417 order, on inlaid ware transitional between late Goryeo celadon and buncheong.
rows.cautions: Only one item known to us (an inlaid maebyeong, NMK 덕수 2723, seen via a glass-plate photograph).

facts.text: The Ŭisŏnggo was a Goryeo royal storehouse continued in early Joseon; in 1403 it was merged into the Naejasi.
An inlaid buncheong maebyeong with 義成庫 incised vertically on the body (NMK 덕수 2723) is cited as early-Joseon inlaid ware.

rows.meaning: Saongbang (later Saongwŏn), the royal kitchen and tableware office.
rows.technique: incised
rows.date_note: Saongbang became the Saongwŏn in 1467; this sherd is undated.
rows.what_it_tells: Ware for the court kitchen office, from Gangjin.
rows.cautions: Single sherd; the museum title says 內贍 but its description reads 司饔.

facts.text: A stamped chrysanthemum celadon base sherd from Gangjin has 司饔 incised inside the foot.
司饔房 is named in the 1417 memorial as an office supplied through the Changhŭnggo; it became the Saongwŏn in 1467.

facts.text: In 1451 the court approved restoring Mujin-gun as Gwangju-mok.
