facts.text: A potter printed as 李段九 left Kwangjuyo (広州窯) in the 1970s and set up the Cheongpa kiln (青波窯); 曹東憲 also left Kwangjuyo.
facts.quote: 広州窯からは、曹東憲、青波窯の李段九

rows.meaning: Dongguk kiln of Bang Cheol-ju (方徹柱, art name Hyeoksan 赫山, b. 1922) at Suha-ri, Sindun-myeon, Icheon, founded 1971.
wares: some white porcelain and buncheong in the 1970s
rows.technique: Not documented in any source read: how (or whether) this maker marked its wares was not found.
rows.date_note: Kiln opened 1971; gas kilns from 1981; still working in 2005 (Nakamura).
rows.what_it_tells: A leading second-generation Icheon celadon studio; it sold through Shinsegae department store from 1974 and to Japanese buyers in bulk in the 1980s, so its wares reached Japan and the West.
rows.cautions: Single source (Nakamura 2005, interviews). Mark form unknown.

facts.text: Bang Cheol-ju (b. 1922, Nonsan) took up pottery in 1967 after a business career and opened the Dongguk kiln at Suha-ri, Sindun-myeon, Icheon, in 1971; after its first successes it was designated a model kiln (示範窯) by the Cultural Properties Administration.
facts.quote: 1971年に念願の窯を利川市新屯面水下里に開く (opened his kiln at Suha-ri, Icheon, in 1971)

facts.text: Dongguk-yo celadon was sold at Shinsegae department store from December 1974, shown at Matsuzakaya Ginza in 1973 and in the 1976 '5,000 Years of Korean Art' exhibition with Yu Geun-hyeong and Ji Sun-tak; gas kilns were added from 1981 and Japanese buyers placed large orders.
facts.quote: 1981年から、方氏も東国釜にガス窯を導入 (from 1981 gas kilns)

rows.meaning: An Dong-o, senior Icheon potter of traditional white porcelain.
rows.technique: Not documented in any source read: how (or whether) this maker marked its wares was not found.
rows.what_it_tells: Traditional-style white porcelain by one of the senior Icheon potters of the 1970s-80s.
rows.cautions: Dates of life and mark form not found. Only two brief mentions.

facts.text: An Dong-o was one of two white-porcelain potters (with Cheon Han-bong) chosen for the 1976 '5,000 Years of Korean Art' exhibition.
facts.quote: 白磁部門では安東五・千漢鳳の二氏 (in white porcelain, An Dong-o and Cheon Han-bong)

facts.text: In 1981 he was, with Roh Seok-gyeong, Cho So-su and Ji Sun-tak, a senior adviser of the Korean Traditional Ceramics Association founded by Icheon potters.
facts.quote: 노석경, 안동오, 조소수, 지순탁 등 원로 전승도예가

rows.meaning: Cheon Han-bong, traditional potter chosen for the white-porcelain section of the 1976 '5,000 Years of Korean Art' exhibition.
rows.technique: Not documented in any source read: how (or whether) this maker marked its wares was not found.
rows.what_it_tells: Traditional-style ware by a potter recognized by 1976.
rows.cautions: Single source; dates and mark form not found.

facts.text: Cheon Han-bong was one of two white-porcelain potters chosen for the 1976 '5,000 Years of Korean Art' exhibition.
facts.quote: 安東五・千漢鳳の二氏

rows.meaning: Shin Sang-ho (b. 1947), contemporary Korean ceramic artist whose celadon draws on Goryeo forms.
rows.technique: incised signature and date on the base (V&A 1990 vase); signed and dated box (Cleveland 1994 jar); the signature's form is not transcribed
rows.date_note: Born 1947 (V&A, Cleveland); the dated museum items are 1990 and 1994. Start of career not researched; 1970 is a placeholder decade, not a sourced date.
rows.what_it_tells: A contemporary studio artist's signed and dated work (not a reproduction workshop). A dated incised signature is normal for him.
rows.cautions: Modern art ceramics; a Goryeo-style design does not make it a reproduction or an antique. Copyrighted museum images (V&A, Cleveland).

facts.text: Shin Sang-ho was born in 1947.
His 1990 faceted inlaid-celadon vase in the V&A has an incised signature and date on the base.
facts.quote: Incised signature and date on base

facts.text: His 1994 'Dream Jar' in the Cleveland Museum of Art has a box signed and dated 1994.
He wrote the survey 『한국도예』 (Hongik University Ceramics Research Institute, 1996), cited by Encykorea's entries on Yu Geun-hyeong, Ji Sun-tak and Hwang In-chun.

rows.meaning: Place mark 'Taegu' (Daegu city) painted on the base of modern celadon.
rows.technique: painted in underglaze iron black
rows.date_note: Date of the one documented example (V&A FE.24-1984, made 1979-84).
rows.what_it_tells: Modern celadon from Daegu; the V&A's example was given by the President of Taegu Junior Technical College, which suggests (not proven) a college or local studio product.
rows.cautions: Single example. The V&A record gives the mark as 'Taegu' and does not say whether it is written in Latin letters, hanja or hangul.

facts.text: A V&A carved celadon vase made 1979-84 bears the mark 'Taegu' in underglaze iron black on the base; the donor was President of Taegu Junior Technical College.

rows.meaning: Seongbuk-dong kiln of the Korean Art Society (한국조형문화연구소), Seoul: a Rockefeller-supported post-war workshop where Yu Geun-hyeong and Ji Sun-tak revived celadon and white porcelain.
rows.technique: Not documented in any source read: how (or whether) this maker marked its wares was not found.
rows.date_note: The Korean Art Society was incorporated in October 1955; the kiln opened in spring 1956 and closed in 1962 (Ahn 2020, citing Jeong Mu-jeong 2019).
rows.what_it_tells: If a mark or label of this kiln is found, the item is a 1956-62 Seoul revival ware, made in the years when Americans in Korea were a main market.
rows.cautions: No mark is described in any source. The link to American buyers is inferred from the Rockefeller funding, not documented.

facts.text: The Seongbuk-dong kiln (城北洞窯, also 澗松窯, 'Kiln of Korean Art Society') of the Korean Art Society was set up with Rockefeller Foundation support; Yu Geun-hyeong worked there as a sculptor-craftsman and Ji Sun-tak made modernised white porcelain there.
facts.quote: 성북동가마(城北洞窯, 澗松窯, Kiln of Korean Art

facts.text: It opened in spring 1956 and closed in 1962.
facts.quote: 1956년 봄 성북동에서 … 개요 (opened at Seongbuk-dong in spring 1956)

rows.meaning: Daebang-dong kiln of the Korean Art Products Research Institute (한국미술품연구소), Seoul, set up by the sculptor Yun Hyo-jung to make export goods in traditional techniques.
wares: celadon and other traditional-style export wares
rows.technique: Not documented in any source read: how (or whether) this maker marked its wares was not found.
rows.date_note: Opened 1956 (autumn 1956 per Encykorea; Ahn 2020), closed 1958 for financial reasons (Encykorea).
rows.what_it_tells: A 1956-58 Seoul export ware: the kiln made goods 'suitable for export'.
rows.cautions: No mark described in any source.

facts.text: The Daebang-dong kiln of the Korean Art Products Research Institute opened in 1956 and closed in 1958 for financial reasons; Yu Geun-hyeong worked in its sculpture section and Ji Sun-tak was factory manager.
facts.quote: 1958년 대방동 가마가 경영난으로 문을 닫게 (in 1958 the Daebang-dong kiln closed for financial reasons)

facts.text: It made export goods in traditional techniques.
facts.quote: 전통기법을 바탕으로 수출에 적합한 상품 (export goods in traditional techniques)

facts.text: It was founded by the sculptor Yun Hyo-jung (尹孝重, 1917-1967).

rows.meaning: Haengnam Company (杏南社, 'southern apricot company'); the crest is an apricot blossom set on a vessel
rows.technique: printed backstamp (gold crest and hangul, green body-name line on the 1983 V&A examples)
rows.where_on_object: underside of cups and saucers, inside the foot ring
rows.date_note: 1942 = founding (the '1942' inside the crest is most likely the founding year, not a production date). The hangul name 행남사 was the company name until it became ㈜행남자기 in 1994; a design historian says the blossom symbol gave way to a gold 'H' in the 1990s. The earliest securely dated example found is the V&A's 1983 Samsung commission. Caution: the company name reverted to 행남사 in 2018-2019, so a modern item can also read 행남사.
rows.what_it_tells: Made by Haengnam (Haengnamsa), Mokpo, South Korea, one of Korea's two big tableware makers. The apricot-blossom crest with 행남사 points to pre-1994 production; with 'Ivory China' it is 1976 or later, with 'Snow Bone China' 1981 or later. 1970s export items carried the blossom with 'Made in Korea'.
rows.cautions: The '1942' in the crest is the founding year, not the date the item was made. 행남사 reappears as the company name from 2018-2019, so check the body name and style. Bone-china start dates are disputed (1957 vs 1971), so 'bone china' wording alone does not prove an early date. From 1989 Haengnam had an Indonesian joint venture (company timeline), so some later Haengnam wares may not be Korean-made. In 1986 Haengnam licensed a trademark from France's Bernardaud (베어나도), and 1990s Haengnam sets used French-sounding names; a French name on an item does not rule out Korean manufacture.

facts.text: Haengnamsa was founded in 1942 in Mokpo by Kim Chang-hun (김창훈).
facts.quote: 고 김창훈 회장이 1942년 목포에서 '행남사'를 창업 (the late chairman Kim Chang-hun founded Haengnamsa in Mokpo in 1942)

facts.text: The name's first syllable 행 is 杏, the apricot tree; the symbol mark is an apricot blossom of five petals and seven stamens resting on a vessel.
facts.quote: 5개의 화판에 7개의 술을 달고 있는 살구꽃 (an apricot blossom with five petals and seven stamens)

facts.text: Haengnam's current logo is described by the company as continuing the early apricot-blossom form.
facts.quote: 초기의 살구꽃 형상을 지속하고 (continues the early apricot-blossom form)

facts.text: In the 1970s Haengnam exported wares bearing the apricot-blossom emblem with 'Made in Korea'.
facts.quote: 살구꽃 문양으로 'Made in Korea'를 달고 (with the apricot-blossom emblem and 'Made in Korea')

facts.text: In the 1990s the company name became 행남자기 and the symbol changed to a gold English initial H.
facts.quote: 심벌은 금빛의 영문 이니셜 H로 바뀐다 (the symbol changes to a gold initial H)

facts.text: The company changed its name from ㈜행남사 to ㈜행남자기 in 1994.
facts.quote: 1994년 '㈜행남사'에서 '㈜행남자기'로 사명을 변경 (1994: renamed from Haengnamsa to Haengnam Jagi)

facts.text: After 2015 the name changed repeatedly: 행남생활건강 (2016), 행남자기 (2017), 행남사 (2018), 스튜디오썸머 (2019), 행남사 (2019); delisted 7 June 2021.
facts.quote: 2018년 '행남사'로 ... 2019년 '행남사'로 변경 (renamed Haengnamsa in 2018 and again in 2019)

facts.text: A V&A coffee cup and saucer made by Haengnam in 1983 for Samsung Electronics carry a base stamp: 'FASHION WARE' over a wreathed blossom-on-vessel emblem with '1942', the body name ('Ivory China' on the saucer, 'Snow Bone China' on the cup) and 행남사.
facts.quote: haengnam stamp at the bottom (V&A catalogue); mark read from V&A base photographs

facts.text: Haengnam opened Korea's first ceramic export (to Hong Kong) in 1963 and began large-scale stoneware exports to the Americas in 1974.
facts.quote: 1974 스톤웨어 국내 최초개발 미주지역 본격적인 수출 (1974: first Korean stoneware, full-scale exports to the Americas)

facts.text: Haengnam set up an Indonesian joint-venture company in 1989.
facts.quote: 1989 인도네시아 현지 합작 투자법인 설립 (1989: Indonesian joint venture set up)

facts.text: In 1986 Haengnam signed a trademark-licensing and technical tie-up with France's Bernardaud; 1990s Haengnam set names included 베어나도.
facts.quote: 프랑스 베어나도사와 상표 도입 및 기술 제휴 (trademark licence and technical tie-up with Bernardaud, France)

rows.meaning: English product names for Haengnam porcelain bodies, printed in the backstamp under the crest
rows.technique: printed backstamp line (green script on the 1983 V&A examples)
rows.date_note: The company timeline gives the year each body was developed: Ivory China 1976, Snow Bone China 1981, Ultra Fine 1985 (5th factory), Elegant bone china 1998. These are earliest possible dates for an item naming that body, not end dates.
rows.what_it_tells: Gives an earliest possible date: a Haengnam item reading 'Ivory China' is 1976 or later; 'Snow Bone China' is 1981 or later.
rows.cautions: Development years come only from the company's own timeline. 'Ultra Fine' and 'Elegant' have not been seen on a documented ware; treat them as product names until a dated example is found.

facts.text: Haengnam developed 'Ivory China' in 1976.
Haengnam developed 'Snow Bone China' in 1981.
facts.quote: 1981 스노우 본차이나 개발 (1981: Snow Bone China developed)

facts.text: Both names appear on dated 1983 Haengnam wares in the V&A (Ivory China on the saucers, Snow Bone China on the cups).
facts.quote: read from V&A base photographs of FE.3-2025 / FE.4-2025

facts.text: Haengnam's fifth factory, completed in 1985, made 'Ultra Fine'; 'Elegant bone china' production began in 1998.
facts.quote: 1985 제5공장 준공(울트라파인 생산) (1985: 5th factory completed, producing Ultra Fine)

facts.text: Haengnam built a dedicated bone-china factory in 1984.
facts.quote: 1984년에는 본차이나 개발 공장을 (in 1984, a bone-china factory)

rows.meaning: Gold initial H for Haengnam Jagi (Haengnam Chinaware), the company name from 1994
rows.technique: printed (gold), as described; on-ware form not seen
rows.date_note: One source dates the switch from the apricot blossom to a gold initial H to 'the 1990s', together with the 1994 rename to 행남자기. No exact year and no end date were found.
rows.what_it_tells: A Haengnam mark with a gold H and/or the name 행남자기 is from the 1990s or later, not from the export era of the 1950s-80s.
rows.cautions: Single source for the H symbol; its exact form on wares is not documented here.

facts.text: In the 1990s the company name became 행남자기 and the symbol changed to a gold English initial H.
facts.quote: 1990년대 들어 사명은'행남자기'로 (in the 1990s the name became Haengnam Jagi)

facts.text: The rename from ㈜행남사 to ㈜행남자기 took place in 1994.

rows.meaning: Hankook Chinaware ('Korea Ceramics'), Cheongju; founded 1943 as Chungbuk Jedosa
wares: export tableware made under foreign brand names (OEM)
rows.technique: printed backstamp (form by date not documented)
rows.date_note: Founded December 1943; took the trade name 한국도자기주식회사 in August 1967 (encyclopedia). A 'Hankook' name mark is therefore not expected before 1967, though the son who joined in 1973 remembers the firm still being called 충북제도사 then. No dated sequence of Hankook backstamps was found in any source.
rows.what_it_tells: Made by Hankook Chinaware of Cheongju, South Korea's largest tableware maker, which advertises itself as the first Korean bone-china maker. On bone china it is most likely 1970s or later; on Super Strong ware, 1988 or later.
rows.cautions: Much Hankook export ware was made under other companies' names (OEM); the firm's chairman named Lenox, and a 2004 interview also named Royal Doulton and Villeroy & Boch as buyers. An item made by Hankook may therefore bear a Western brand, not 'Hankook'. Hankook also ran three factories in Indonesia (2004), so Hankook-marked ware can be Indonesian-made. Sources disagree on when its bone china began (1973; a request in the mid-1970s, i.e. by 1974; or a 1982 breakthrough), and Korea.net wrongly names Kim Dong-soo (the founder's son) as founder.

facts.text: Hankook Chinaware was founded in December 1943 (60th anniversary on 4 Dec 2003).
It was founded in Cheongju by Kim Jong-ho (김종호), grandfather of the current head; his son Kim Dong-soo later led it.
facts.quote: 고 김종호 회장이 1943년 충북 청주에서 한국도자기를 창업 (the late Kim Jong-ho founded Hankook in Cheongju in 1943)

facts.text: The founder's business began as a small earthenware/pottery works.
facts.quote: 충북에서 질그릇을 굽던 아버지 (his father, who fired earthenware in North Chungcheong)

facts.text: The firm's founding name was Chungbuk Jedosa (충북제도사).
facts.quote: '충북제도사'라고 불리는 작은 회사 (a small firm called Chungbuk Jedosa)

facts.text: The trade name became 한국도자기주식회사 in August 1967.
facts.quote: 1967년 8월 한국도자기주식회사로 상호를 변경 (Aug 1967 renamed Hankook Dojagi Co.)

facts.text: Bone-china start is disputed: JoongAng Daily gives 1973; the 2004 Kim Sung-soo interview says the First Lady asked for it 'around the mid-1970s' and that it succeeded in 1982; the encyclopedia records a bone-china plant expansion in July 1981 and KS certification for bone china in September 1989.
facts.quote: 1982년, ... 동양 최초로 본차이나 개발에 성공 (1982: succeeded in developing the Orient's first bone china)

facts.text: Most Hankook exports were OEM, sold under foreign makers' names such as Lenox.
facts.quote: '레녹스'사와 '시스락' 등 외국 도자기업체의 이름으로 납품 (supplied under the names of foreign makers such as Lenox)

facts.text: A 2004 interview also names Royal Doulton (UK) and Villeroy & Boch (Germany) among foreign sellers supplied.
facts.quote: 영국의 '로열덜튼', 독일의 '빌레로이 보흐' (Britain's Royal Doulton, Germany's Villeroy & Boch)

facts.text: In 2004 Hankook had seven factories in Cheongju and three in Indonesia, the latter mainly making export goods.
facts.quote: 인도네시아에도 3개의 공장 (three factories in Indonesia as well)

rows.meaning: Hankook's bone-ash strengthened porcelain body, cheaper than bone china
rows.technique: printed backstamp line (form not documented in a source)
rows.date_note: Development year disputed: 1988 (2004 interview with the company head) vs 1991 (Korea Times 2013). By 1996 Super Strong made up 60% of output (encyclopedia).
rows.what_it_tells: A Hankook item naming Super Strong is 1988 or later, so it is not from the 1950s-70s.
rows.cautions: The exact backstamp wording has not been seen in a dated source; it is known only from seller listing titles.

facts.text: Hankook developed the Super Strong body, containing cattle bone, in 1988.
facts.quote: 1988년, ... '슈퍼스트롱'을 세계 최초로 개발 (1988: developed Super Strong, a world first)

facts.text: Korea Times dates Super Strong to 1991.
facts.quote: developed in 1991 a new tableware body

facts.text: At the end of 1996 Hankook's output was 40% bone china and 60% Super Strong.

rows.meaning: Hankook Chinaware's premium bone-china brand
rows.technique: printed backstamp (form not documented here)
rows.date_note: Launched July 2003 (Money Today, Dec 2003; JoongAng and Korea Times also say 2003); Korea.net says 2004. Prouna Jewelry line 2007.
rows.what_it_tells: Prouna-marked bone china is Hankook Chinaware's and dates from 2003 or later; it is not a vintage mark.
rows.cautions: Modern brand; a Prouna item in an estate is 21st-century.

facts.text: Prouna was launched in July 2003, co-planned with a Royal Doulton designer.
facts.quote: 지난 7월 출시한 '프라우나' (Prouna, launched this past July [2003])

facts.text: Korea.net gives 2004 as Prouna's launch year.
facts.quote: launched a new premium brand, Prouna

rows.meaning: Kwangjuyo, 'the Gwangju kiln', a ceramics company in Icheon founded in 1963 by Cho So-su
rows.technique: not documented (no source describes how early Kwangjuyo wares were marked)
rows.date_note: Founded 1963 (two independent sources); the founder's son Cho Tae-kwon took over in 1988. Items would date 1963 or later.
rows.what_it_tells: A Kwangjuyo item is a modern Korean studio-factory ware from Icheon, made 1963 or later in historical styles (celadon, buncheong, white porcelain). It is not a Goryeo or Joseon antique.
rows.cautions: The hanja (廣州窯 vs 光州窯) and the form of Kwangjuyo's mark have not been established from any source read. Do not confuse with the historical Gwangju (廣州) royal kilns of the Joseon court (closed 1883): a Joseon-period reference to 廣州 means the royal kiln district, not this company. Icheon kilns, Kwangjuyo among them, grew from 1965 on Japanese tourist and souvenir demand for reproductions of Goryeo celadon and Joseon white porcelain. Founding date conflict: 1963 (company-related sources) vs Yu Geun-hyeong working at 'Kwangjuyo' from 1959 (Encykorea). Nakamura writes the name 広州窯 (= 廣州窯) in Japanese, which supports 廣州窯 but is not a company source.

facts.text: Kwangjuyo was founded in 1963 by Cho So-su (조소수); his son Cho Tae-kwon took it over in 1988.
facts.quote: 고 조소수 창업주가 1963년 설립한 광주요 (Kwangjuyo, founded in 1963 by the late founder Cho So-su)

facts.text: Kwangjuyo's factory is in Icheon, Gyeonggi Province.
facts.quote: 경기도 이천의 광주요 (Kwangjuyo of Icheon, Gyeonggi)

facts.text: Cho So-su took over an existing wood-fired kiln at Sugwang-ri, Icheon (built 1949, rebuilt 1962 as a 12-chamber climbing kiln), which stands behind Kwangjuyo's ceramics center.
facts.quote: 기존의 장작가마를 인수해 지금의 형태로 (took over the existing wood kiln and gave it its present form)

facts.text: Cho So-su was among the potters who reproduced Goryeo celadon and Joseon white porcelain at Sindun-myeon, Icheon; Kwangjuyo is named as one of the area's first-generation kilns.
facts.quote: 유근형, 지순탁, 조소수 등이 ... 고려청자와 조선백자를 재현 (Yu Geun-hyeong, Ji Sun-tak, Cho So-su and others reproduced Goryeo celadon and Joseon white porcelain)

facts.text: Icheon's ceramics industry boomed after 1965 Korea-Japan normalization, as Japanese visitors sought ceramics as souvenirs.
facts.quote: 일본인들이 관광기념품으로 도자를 찾으면서 (as Japanese sought ceramics as tourist souvenirs)

facts.text: In 1993 Kwangjuyo fired everyday ware in gas kilns while also making buncheong and celadon in a traditional climbing kiln.
facts.quote: 생활도자기를 가스가마에서 구워내는 광주요 (Kwangjuyo, which fires everyday ware in gas kilns)

facts.text: The company cites a 1966 white porcelain jar with an underglaze copper-red ('cinnabar') grape design made by the founder as its design starting point.
facts.quote: 1966 White Porcelain Jar with Cinnabar Grape Design

facts.text: The Joseon royal kiln branch at Gwangju (廣州分院) closed in 1883.
facts.quote: 1883년(고종 20)에 광주 분원(廣州分院)이 폐쇄 (1883: the Gwangju branch kiln was closed)

facts.text: Encykorea's Yu Geun-hyeong entry says that from 1959 Yu worked at 'the Kwangjuyo at Sugwang-ri, Icheon', earlier than the 1963 founding year given in company-related sources; the name may be applied retrospectively to the Sugwang-ri kiln that Cho So-su later took over.
facts.quote: 이듬해부터 … 수광리의 광주요로 (from the next year, to Kwangjuyo at Sugwang-ri)

facts.text: Nakamura writes the company as 広州窯 (the Japanese form of 廣州窯) and names 曹東憲 and a founder of 青波窯 as potters who left it in the 1970s.
facts.quote: 広州窯からは、曹東憲 (from Kwangjuyo, Cho Dong-heon)

rows.meaning: English-language country-of-origin mark naming Korea, the form that US import law asks for (written in English, not hangul).
wares: any imported article (export and souvenir ceramics, metalwork, lacquer and the rest): the law covers all foreign goods, not one ware
rows.technique: Any reasonable method is allowed: printing, stenciling, stamping, branding or labeling (1938 Act). On items it can be painted, printed, stamped, impressed, or a paper or foil label.
rows.where_on_object: The law asks for 'a conspicuous place' on the article, or on the container where allowed. No source was found on where Korean makers usually put it.
rows.date_note: No date range is possible. US Customs accepted 'Korea' for goods of Japanese-ruled Korea by 1935 (and in a 1940 list), and CBP accepted 'Made in Korea' in 2025. The word alone spans the colonial period and today.
rows.what_it_tells: The item, or its label or box, was marked for export to a market with origin-marking rules (the US from 1891; Canada from 1922), and Korea was declared as the country of origin. It does not date the item, separate pre-1945 from post-1945 work, or say who made it. Adding 'Made in' changes nothing for dating: US statutes never required those words.
rows.cautions: 1) 'Made in' is no date test. It was never required by US statute, and today it is required only when another place name appears on the article. 2) Origin follows customs rules, not every step of manufacture: CBP held Chinese squid seasoned in Korea to be Chinese, and mixed kits must name each part's origin. 3) Removable paper origin labels are how new items get passed off as old (warning written about Nippon, but it applies generally). 4) No source was found that dates Korean 'Korea' paper or foil stickers, or ties sticker styles to decades.

facts.text: The McKinley Tariff Act (approved Oct. 1, 1890), section 6, required from March 1, 1891 that foreign articles of a kind usually marked, and all packages of imported goods, be plainly marked in legible English words showing the country of origin. Unmarked goods were refused entry.

The Tariff Act of Oct. 3, 1913 (sec. IV, para. F, subsec. 1) required all foreign articles capable of being marked to be marked in legible English words to show the country of origin (as quoted by the Treasury in 1914). The 1909 Act's marking clause (sec. 7) is cited in the 1917 digest but its text was not read.
facts.quote: capable of being marked (1913 Act, as quoted)

facts.text: The Customs Administrative Act of 1938 rewrote sec. 304. Articles must be marked conspicuously and permanently so as to show an ultimate purchaser in the US the English name of the country of origin, and the Treasury may decide by regulation which words and abbreviations are acceptable. This is still the text of 19 U.S.C. 1304(a).
facts.quote: English name of the country of origin

facts.text: No US marking statute read here (1890, 1913, 1938) requires the words 'Made in'. Current CBP guidance requires 'made in' only when another locality name appears on the article. A collector site states that the 'Made in' prefix was never a US requirement.
facts.quote: “made in” is required only in the case (CBP)

facts.text: Under Japanese rule, US Customs accepted 'Korea' as well as 'Chosen'. A 1935 Bureau of Customs ruling held that goods made in Chosen may be marked 'Chosen' or 'Korea', and the Bureau's 1940 marking bulletin lists 'Chosen or Korea' as the acceptable marking.

Today CBP accepts 'Korea' for South Korean goods. A Nov. 2025 ruling found 'Made in Korea' and 'Product of Korea' acceptable for a South Korean product, and a 2026 ruling's model marking uses 'made in Korea' for South Korean components.

The regulation requires the full English country name, but accepts abbreviations that unmistakably indicate the country and variant spellings that clearly indicate the English name. Neither the regulation nor CBP's guide gives a Korean example, so the status of 'S. Korea' or 'R.O.K.' was not established here.
facts.quote: full English name of the country (134.45)

facts.text: Origin is a customs judgment. Squid salted in China and seasoned in Korea was ruled Chinese origin, and kits mixing Korean and Chinese parts must name each part's country.
facts.quote: country of origin of each component

facts.text: A reproduction specialist warns that 'Made in ...' origin marks on new wares are usually removable paper stickers, and that removing them is how new items are misrepresented.

rows.meaning: Korea, under the English name the Japanese colonial Government-General used ('Chosen'). US Customs accepted it as a country-of-origin marking.
rows.technique: as for any origin mark (printed, stamped, label)
rows.date_note: From the August 1910 annexation, when the colonial government began calling Korea 'Chosen' in English. US Customs acceptance is attested in 1935 and 1940. The end of the name at liberation (1945) is not sourced here.
rows.what_it_tells: An English 'CHOSEN' origin mark points to goods exported while Korea was under Japanese rule. 'Korea' was equally acceptable at that time, so an item marked 'Korea' is not shown to be post-1945 just because it lacks 'Chosen'.
rows.cautions: No dated item with a 'Chosen' origin mark was found in the sources read. Whether 'Japan' alone was accepted for Korean goods before 1935 is unknown: the 1935 ruling 'extended' an earlier decision (T.D. 47292-1) whose text was not seen. 'Chosen' is also the ordinary English word, which makes text searches noisy.

facts.text: Japan annexed Korea in August 1910 (treaty concluded Aug. 22, 1910).
The colonial Government-General published its English reports under the name 'Chosen (Korea)', using 'Chosen' as the country's English name.
US Customs accepted either 'Chosen' or 'Korea' on goods made in Chosen: a 1935 ruling, and the 1940 marking-bulletin list, where both the Chosen and Korea entries read 'Chosen or Korea'.
The 1935 ruling says it extends an earlier decision, T.D. 47292-1, so Customs had ruled on the marking of goods from Chosen before late 1935. That earlier text was not found.
In the same 1940 list, Japan's other colony Formosa had the acceptable marking 'Formosa or Taiwan', and Japan's was 'Japan'. Chosen and Korea were listed only as 'Chosen or Korea'.

rows.meaning: Japanese name for Japan (日本), used as the origin mark on Japanese exports to the US. It is NOT a Korean mark. It is here because the 1921 'Nippon' rule is the model behind collectors' dating by country name, and to separate law from lore.
wares: Japanese export goods: porcelain, cutlery, brushes and others named in the rulings
rows.technique: printed or stamped backstamps; die-sunk on cutlery (T.D. 37828)
rows.where_on_object: usually the base on porcelain (collector literature); not researched further
rows.date_note: The marking law took effect March 1, 1891. The Treasury formally accepted 'Nippon' only by T.D. 34740 of Aug. 31, 1914, noting that ports had treated it differently before. A Treasury decision dated March 1, 1921 withdrew acceptance, effective six months later (about Sept. 1, 1921), with time allowed to sell off goods already marked. The 1921 end is therefore soft.
rows.what_it_tells: For comparison only. 'Nippon' points to Japanese manufacture for the US market, roughly 1891-1921. Collectors' blanket rule (Nippon = 1891-1921, Japan = after 1921) rests on real Treasury decisions, but the exact cut-off date differs between collector books.
rows.cautions: Fake 'Nippon' marks have appeared on new porcelain since the 1980s and 1990s. They are legal if the true origin is also marked, often on a removable paper label. A Korean item should not be dated by analogy with the Nippon rule: no matching Korea-specific ruling was found.

facts.text: T.D. 34740 (Aug. 31, 1914) noted 'a variance in practice at the several ports'. It ruled that Japanese articles marked 'Nippon' were legally marked under the 1913 Act, because the word was commonly used in the US for Japan.
facts.quote: may now be considered as incorporated

facts.text: T.D. 37828 (Dec. 9, 1918) extended this to cutlery die-sunk 'Nippon' plus the maker's or purchaser's name. A 1920 congressional tariff summary still listed 'Nippon' as sufficient.

In 1921 the Treasury reversed itself. A decision dated March 1, 1921 held 'Nippon' not to comply with the law and revoked T.D. 34740 and 37828, effective six months from that date. A trade weekly of April 13, 1921 reported that Japanese articles 'must be marked Japan instead of Nippon', with time allowed for stock already marked.

Collector books give different cut-off dates: Van Patten's 1979, 1984 and 2001 books say Sept. 1, 1921, her 2005 book says Oct. 1, 1921, and others say March 1921. The decision as she quotes it is dated March 1, 1921 and effective six months later.
Canada's 1921 customs branding amendment also required origin marks in English or French and refused foreign-language names 'such as Nippon for Japan'.
facts.quote: such as Nippon for Japan, will not be

facts.text: The common dating rule (Nippon c. 1891-1921; 'Japan' or 'Made in Japan' after 1921) is repeated by an archaeology lab citing a collector book, and by collector sites. It is lore built on the rulings above, not a law in itself.
Since the 1980s and mid-1990s, new porcelain has carried faked Nippon marks. This is legal if the real origin is marked, often only by a removable paper label.

rows.meaning: A supposed export mark for US-occupied southern Korea (1945-48). NOT attested: no source for it was found.
rows.date_note: Unattested. For comparison, SCAP ordered 'Made in Occupied Japan' on Japanese exports by a directive of Feb. 20, 1947.
rows.what_it_tells: Nothing reliable yet. No customs ruling, occupation directive or collector reference to an 'Occupied Korea' mark was found. Treat such a mark as unverified until a dated example or document turns up.
rows.cautions: Do not carry the 'Occupied Japan' rule over to Korea. The SCAP directive was addressed to the Japanese government only. Dates for 'Occupied Japan' marks also differ: the directive is dated Feb. 1947, while guides start such marks in 1945.

facts.text: 'Made in Occupied Japan' is documented. On Feb. 20, 1947, SCAP directed that every article prepared for export from Japan, its container and outer package be marked in legible English 'Made in Occupied Japan'. An archaeology lab dates such marked ceramics 1945-1952.
facts.quote: with the words "Made in Occupied Japan."

facts.text: The directive was addressed to the Imperial Japanese Government and covers Japanese exports; it says nothing about Korea.

rows.chars: 京城李王家美術工場造
rows.meaning: 'Made by the Yi Royal House Art Workshop, Keijō (Seoul)': maker's inscription of the royal-household art workshop (李王職美術品製作所, Iwangjik Misulpum Jejakso).
rows.technique: Inscription together with a mark; Kim calls it '미명 마크' and does not describe its form.
rows.date_note: Yi Royal Household (李王家) naming implies 1910 or later; the Yiwangjik period ended with incorporation on 16 Aug 1922. Kim (2021) places this set in the Yiwangjik period, before Princess Deokhye's 1931 wedding.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the royal-household art workshop in Seoul as maker. Per Kim, mark and inscription together identify the item as made in the Iwangjik-workshop period, before the workshop's commercial takeover.
rows.cautions: Single source chain: Kim 2021 relies on Jeong Ji-hee's 2016 dissertation. Only one item is reported (a silver miniature set among Princess Deokhye's trousseau items). The wording 李王家美術工場 differs from the workshop's formal name 李王職美術品製作所. No fineness mark is reported. The phrase '미명 마크' in Kim's note (an unexplained mark accompanying the inscription) is not described; ask the Kyushu National Museum or consult Jeong Ji-hee 2016/2018 for its form.

facts.text: A silver miniature set (은제소꿉) among Princess Deokhye's trousseau items in the Kyushu National Museum bears the inscription 京城李王家美術工場造. Its mark and inscription identify it as made in the Iwangjik workshop period.
facts.quote: 李王家美術工場造) 명 은제소꿉: silver toy set so inscribed

facts.text: The Iwangjik workshop succeeded the Hanseong Art Products Workshop (run 1908-1913), made royal wares alongside commercial sales, and in the early 1920s passed to the privately run Joseon Misulpum Jejakso Co.

rows.chars: 京城 朝鮮美術品製作所造 京城太平通
rows.rr: Gyeongseong Joseon Misulpum Jejakso jo, Gyeongseong Taepyeongtong
rows.mr: Kyŏngsŏng Chosŏn Misulp'um Chejakso cho, Kyŏngsŏng T'aep'yŏngt'ong
rows.meaning: 'Made by the Chosen Art Products Manufactory, Keijō (Seoul), Taepyeong-tong': printed maker's paper label, with the item name 神仙爐 (sinseollo).
rows.technique: printed paper label
rows.date_note: Company period: 16 Aug 1922 to its dissolution on 13 July 1936 (sillokwiki), or c.1937 (Encykorea; Choi Bum). The NFMK sinseollo is dated 1920s-30s.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the maker and its Seoul street address. It is a domestic maker's label, not an export origin mark and not a fineness mark.
rows.cautions: Single source. Paper labels are fragile and removable; a label proves the label, not the item it is now on.

facts.text: A cupronickel sinseollo of the 1920s-30s in the National Folk Museum of Korea, made by Joseon Misulpum Jejakso Co., has a paper label on the lid top printed '神仙爐' and '京城 朝鮮美術品製作所造 京城太平通'.
facts.quote: 京城 朝鮮美術品製作所造 京城太平通

facts.text: Joseon Misulpum Jejakso Co., a private company that took over the Iwangjik workshop in the early 1920s, presented itself in advertisements (e.g. Chosen Shinbun, Nov. 27, 1931) as the Iwangjik's successor.
facts.quote: 이왕직의 후신임을: as the Iwangjik's successor

facts.text: The company was formed on 16 August 1922 as a private joint-stock company taking over the Yiwangjik workshop and held its dissolution meeting on 13 July 1936; Encykorea and Choi Bum say it ran to about 1937.

The company also made a pavilion-design vase now in the Amorepacific Museum (Kim, n.44) and produced mother-of-pearl lacquer, gold and silver work, bronze castings, brushes and ink, stone and wood-and-shell work.
facts.quote: 나전칠기(螺鈿漆器), 금은세공품(金銀細工品), 청동주물

caveats: Korean dates before 1896-01-01 are in the lunar calendar. A lunar year begins between about 21 January and 20 February, so dates in the 11th and especially the 12th lunar month (and the last days of the year) usually fall in January-February of the next Western year. Catalogues and the Sillok normally label the whole lunar year with the Western year in which it mostly falls (e.g. 세종 1년 기해 = 1419), so 'dated 1438' for a 12th-month event can mean early 1439. After 1896 official documents are solar, but temples, families and private inscriptions often kept lunar months (e.g. 1901: painted 광무 5년 10월 28일, consecrated in 동짓달 11월 20일).

Years follow the Korean sources' own count. reign_start/reign_end = Western years of accession and end as given by the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (the usual Western-table convention). year1 = the Western year of the king's 元年 (1년) as the Goryeosa (NIKH database) or the Sillok labels it. Korean official history used 踰年稱元法 (유년칭원법): the accession year stays with the predecessor (labelled 卽位年), and 元年 is the next year. Exceptions where the accession year itself is 元年 (즉위년칭원): dynastic founders (Goryeo 太祖 918, Joseon 太祖 1392) and kings who replaced a deposed or abdicating ruler (Joseon 世祖 1455, 中宗 1506, 仁祖 1623; Goryeo 恭讓王 1389). To convert 'KING n年' use year1 + n − 1; '卽位年' = accession_year.

Contemporary Goryeo inscriptions did not always follow the Goryeosa count: 光宗 officially used 卽位年稱元 in 949 and 顯宗 revived it, so a regnal year on a 10th-11th-century Goryeo item may be one year earlier than the Goryeosa-based conversion. Temple names are posthumous: any inscription that names a king by temple name was written after his death (and for 英祖/正祖/純祖/端宗 after the dates the names were given). Many temple names repeat between the dynasties (太祖 定宗 文宗 成宗 睿宗 仁宗 明宗 肅宗 顯宗 景宗 高宗); check the dynasty before converting.

counts.label: the Chongzhen count
counts.explain: After the Ming fell, Joseon writers kept counting from the Ming's last era, Chongzhen (1628–1644), rather than write Qing era names: 崇禎紀元後三甲子 is the third gapja year after 1628, 1804. An ordinal (再 second, 三 third …) counts that cyclical year's returns from 1629. For the sixteen cyclical years that also fell in 1629–1644, and for 戊辰 (1628), writers counted two ways, so two years are given. Without an ordinal the cycle is not stated. The count was used into the 20th century, so a 崇禎 date is a loyalist's choice of words, not a sign of the 17th century.

counts.research: 'After the beginning of the Chongzhen era' — the Ming loyalist count used by Joseon literati, families and some temples after 1637-1644, when Qing eras became official. 崇禎元年 = 1628 (戊辰). 崇禎紀元後 N年 (numeral + 年, often followed by the ganji): AD = 1627 + N (N counts 1628 as year 1) 崇禎紀元後 + ordinal + ganji (再 = 2nd, 三 = 3rd … 六; also 二, N周, 周甲 = 2nd, 歲次 may intervene: 崇禎紀元後歲次五丙子): The N-th occurrence of that ganji year counting from 1629 (i.e. the first one after 1628). For 43 of the 60 ganji the first occurrence is after 1644 and the reading is unambiguous: AD = (first year ≥ 1629 with that ganji) + 60·(N − 1). ordinal + one of the 16 ganji that also fell inside the Chongzhen reign 1629-1644 (己巳 庚午 辛未 壬申 癸酉 甲戌 乙亥 丙子 丁丑 戊寅 己卯 庚辰 辛巳 壬午 癸未 甲申): Two conventions. A (majority): count the 1629-1644 occurrence as the first — AD = y1 + 60·(N − 1). C (minority): skip it and count from 1645 — AD = y1 + 60·N. Give both candidates; A first. ordinal + 戊辰 (1628 itself): Two conventions: exclusive (first 戊辰 = 1688, so 再戊辰 = 1748) or inclusive (1628 is the first, so 三戊辰 = 1748). Give both: 1628 + 60·(N − 1) and 1688 + 60·(N − 1). 崇禎紀元後 / 崇禎後 + ganji with NO ordinal (often 崇禎後歲次甲戌…): The cycle is not stated; any post-1644 year with that ganji is possible. Resolve from the person, office or event named. Do not assume the first cycle. N周 + ganji / 周甲 + N年: N周X behaves like ordinal N (崇禎紀元後五周甲辰 = 1904, 甲峰遺稿 printed 1904; 三周庚寅 = 1770 金鍾厚). 周甲 alone = one full cycle later (崇禎後周甲戊辰 = 1688, 南九萬). 周甲 + N年 = 60 + N years: 崇禎紀元後周甲四十五年壬子 = 1627 + 105 = 1732. N甲子 followed by 歲次 + another ganji (崇禎紀元後三甲子歲次丙午): Here 三甲子 names the 60-year cycle, not a year; the year is the following ganji within that cycle (鄭赫臣 1719-1793: 丙午 = 1786). Read the whole phrase before converting. A 崇禎 date is a political choice, not a sign of 17th-century date: the count was still used in 1917 and later. Printing prefaces are often dated years before or after the actual print (compare ITKC 간행년). Do not confuse 崇禎紀元後 dates with the hall name 崇政殿 (경희궁).

counts.label: the Chongzhen count in years
counts.explain: 崇禎紀元後 with a number of years counts 1628 as year 1: 崇禎紀元後百年 is 1727. 周甲 adds a cycle of sixty: 崇禎紀元後周甲四十五年 is 1732.

counts.label: 崇禎後 with a number of years
counts.explain: Written 崇禎後 without 紀元, a number of years was counted from 1628, 1644 or 1645 by different writers; the cyclical year written with it decides.

counts.label: the count from the fall of the Ming
counts.explain: 崇禎甲申後 counts from the fall of the Ming in 1644 (甲申): most writers made 1644 year 1, some 1645.

counts.label: the Yongli count
counts.explain: A few loyalists counted from the Southern Ming era Yongli (1647–1662) the same way: 永歷五辛亥 is the fifth sinhae year after 1647, 1911.

counts.label: Dangi years
counts.explain: Years from the legendary founding of Korea by Dangun in 2333 BC: subtract 2333 (檀紀4281 is 1948). Official in South Korea from 1948 to 1961, and used privately before and after.

counts.label: years of the Republic
counts.explain: Years of the Republic from 1919 (the Provisional Government): 大韓民國三十年 is 1948. Found in documents, not yet on items.

counts.label: Juche years
counts.explain: North Korea's count from 1912, Kim Il-sung's birth year: 주체86 is 1997. Used from 1997.

counts.label: Buddhist years
counts.explain: Buddhist years. Korean temples once counted from 1027 BC (佛紀2950 is 1923); since 1956 the count is 544 years ahead (佛紀2570 is 2026). A 29xx year is the old count.

foreign_eras.text: 918–933: Goryeo own era 天授
933–938: Later Tang 後唐 (長興, 應順, 淸泰). 933, 3rd month: investiture by Later Tang, its era adopted
938–948: Later Jin 後晉 (天福, 開運). 938, 7th month
948–951: Later Han 後漢 (乾祐) — overlapping Goryeo 光德 950-951. 948, 9th month
951–963: Later Zhou 後周 (廣順, 顯德) — overlapping Goryeo 光德 (to 952/3?) and 峻豐 960-963. 951, 12th month
963–994: Song 宋 (乾德 … 淳化). 963, 12th month
994–1016: Liao 遼/契丹 (統和, 開泰). 994, 2nd month
1022–1116: Liao 遼 (太平, 重熙 from 1038, 淸寧, 咸雍, 太康, 太安, 壽隆, 乾統, 天慶). 1022, 4th month: investiture by Liao
1116–1126: no foreign era in official documents: Liao 天慶 dropped, ganji only. 1116, 4th month

1126–1224: Jin 金 (天會, 天眷, 皇統, 天德, 貞元, 正隆, 大定, 明昌, 承安, 泰和, 大安, 崇慶, 至寧, 貞祐, 興定, 元光, 正大). 1126, 4th month: Goryeo declared itself a vassal (稱臣) of Jin; 1142, 5th month: Jin invested the king. The Goryeosa table does not give an explicit date for adopting the Jin era (gap).
1224–1260: Jin era abandoned ("as Jin declined"); no foreign era recorded until 1260. 1224
1260–1369: Mongol/Yuan 元 (中統, 至元, 元貞, 大德, 至大, 皇慶, 延祐, 至治, 泰定, 天曆, 至順, 元統, 至元, 至正). 1260, 8th month: 中統 adopted

1369–1392: Ming 明 洪武 — stopped 至正 in the 5th month of 1369, adopted 洪武 in the 7th month of 1370; Northern Yuan 宣光 from the 2nd month of 1377 to the 9th month of 1378; 洪武 halted in the 4th month of 1388 and restored in the 6th month of 1388
1392–1637: Ming 明 eras (洪武 … 崇禎)

1637–1894: Qing 淸 eras (崇德, 順治, 康熙, 雍正, 乾隆, 嘉慶, 道光, 咸豐, 同治, 光緖) in official documents. The 1637 surrender terms required Joseon to give up the Ming era; after months of non-compliance King Injo ordered 崇德 for public documents. Diaries record its use from the 4th month of 1637 (丁丑): 夏四月行用崇德年號 / 夏四月。始用崇德年號。傳曰。吏曹書崇德.
1894–1895: 開國 count (see korean_eras)
1896–1910: 建陽 / 光武 / 隆熙 (see korean_eras)

1910–1945: Japanese eras 明治 (to 45 = 1912), 大正 (元年 1912 - 15 = 1926), 昭和 (元年 1926 - 20 = 1945). 明治元年 = 1868; 大正 replaced 明治 in the 7th month of 明治45 (1912); 昭和 replaced 大正 in the 12th month of 大正15 (1926). So 1912 can be written 明治四十五年 or 大正元年, and 1926 大正十五年 or 昭和元年.
1945–1948: Western calendar (西紀) under the U.S. military government
1948–1961: 檀紀 (Dangi) official in the Republic of Korea (see special_counts)
1962–today: Western calendar (西紀) official from 1962-01-01

wares.title: Korean ceramics by period: what each ware is, how to recognize it, and the copies

rows.name: Three Kingdoms (Silla, Gaya) and Unified Silla stoneware
rows.hanja: 新羅土器 · 陶質土器
rows.date_note: encykorea: Silla pottery 'from the late 3rd century to the fall of Silla'; hard high-fired stoneware dominates from the 5th century.
kilns: Gyeongju area, North Gyeongsang (kiln clusters around Cheonbuk-myeon) for Silla wares
Unified Silla glazed wares also at provincial kilns: Guryong-ri (Dangjin, South Chungcheong), Jinjuk-ri (Boryeong, South Chungcheong), Gurim-ri (Yeongam, South Jeolla)
rows.what_it_is: High-fired, mostly unglazed gray stoneware made in Silla and Gaya for tombs and daily use: footed cups with cut-out windows, long-necked jars, stands and figural vessels. After unification (676) shapes became lower and more practical, stamped decoration spread, and a small group of lead-glazed green wares and urns for cremated remains was made.
how_to_recognize: Body: dense, hard gray to blue-gray or gray-black stoneware fired in reduction above about 1,200 °C (Jeong); 'hard as cast iron'.
Surface: usually unglazed; patches of accidental ash glaze and dark smoky marks from the wood kiln are normal.
Decoration: 5th–6th c. incised triangles and compass-drawn semicircles; from about 600 onward small stamped motifs (inhwa) — rings, semicircles, flowers, beads.
Forms: stem cups (gobae) with cut-out windows in the foot, long-necked jars, vessel stands; rare figural vessels (horse and rider, mythical beasts, boats, shoes).
Green lead glaze (Unified Silla): low-fired at about 700–800 °C on a soft gray or reddish body; used only on special items such as cinerary urns and cup-stands.

facts.text: Silla and Gaya pottery of the Three Kingdoms period was fired in reduction at over 1,200 °C, gray-blue-black on the surface and very hard.
facts.quote_gloss: as hard as cast iron

facts.text: Encykorea defines Silla pottery as the wares made and used from the late 3rd century until the fall of Silla (935); typical Silla-style stoneware is established in the early 5th century.
facts.quote_gloss: roughly from the late 3rd century to the fall of Silla

facts.text: Stamped decoration (inhwa-mun) appears by the early 7th century at the latest, so a stamped item is not automatically post-unification (older literature treated stamped ware as the mark of Unified Silla).
facts.quote_gloss: by the early 7th century stamped decoration appears

facts.text: Lead glaze (green) melts at about 700–800 °C, so lead-glazed items are low-fired soft gray or reddish wares; it was used only on special items from Unified Silla to Goryeo.
facts.quote_gloss: melting range about 700–800 °C

facts.text: Wood-kiln firing leaves smoky black swirling marks on the purplish-brown 'skin' of Unified Silla storage vessels (Cleveland label).
facts.quote: smoky black swirling marks that occurred during the firing

examples.title: 도기 기마인물형 명기 (pair of horse-and-rider vessels), Silla 5th c.
도기 기마인물형 뿔잔 (horse-and-rider horn cup), Three Kingdoms 5th c.
녹유골호 (green-glazed cinerary urn with stone case), Unified Silla 8th c.
도기 연유인화문 항아리 일괄 (lead-glazed stamped jars), Unified Silla 8th c.
Vessel with Knobbed Lid, 676–935, stoneware
Burial Urn with Stamped Design, 500s–600s, stamped under olive-green glaze

rows.name: Early celadon (halo-foot bowls) and coarse green celadon
rows.date_note: Start disputed: Jeong (encykorea) puts the first Korean celadon in the later 9th century under Yue influence; the earliest dated whole item is a jar of 993 (淳化四年). Halo-foot bowls typical of the 10th–11th c.
kilns: Daegu-myeon, Gangjin County, South Jeolla (Yongun-ri, Gyeyul-ri) — the largest early group
Wonsan-ri, Baecheon County, South Hwanghae (North Korea); Seo-ri, Idong-myeon, Yongin, Gyeonggi; Wonheung-dong, Goyang, Gyeonggi; Yonggye-ri, Gochang, North Jeolla
Coarse green celadon (nokcheongja): Gyeongseo-dong, Incheon; Sani-myeon, Haenam, South Jeolla (over 50 kilns)
rows.what_it_is: The first Korean celadons, made under the influence of Chinese Yue ware from Zhejiang, at kilns on the west and south coasts. The typical item is a tea bowl with a broad 'halo' foot. Alongside them a cheap, coarse olive-green celadon (nokcheongja) was made in quantity for ordinary use.
how_to_recognize: Foot: the 'halo foot' (haemurigup) — a broad, flat foot ring with a wide contact surface and a small recessed center, so the base looks like a sun with a halo; bowls also have a shallow circular groove cut inside the bottom.
Glaze: often not yet the later gray-green; olive, dark green, yellow-brown or green-brown where reduction failed.
Coarse green celadon: sandy, porous body with grit; glaze close to an ash glaze, green-brown and uneven.
Firing: good early kilns already used saggars (protective clay boxes).

facts.text: A 'halo-foot bowl' (haemurigup wan) has a broad foot ring and a circular groove cut inside the bottom; the name comes from the base looking like the sun with a halo.
facts.quote_gloss: halo-foot bowl

facts.text: Early celadon kilns in Gangjin produced, besides well-reduced 'early bisaek' wares, items fired between reduction and oxidation that came out dark green, green, yellow-brown or green-brown.
facts.quote_gloss: dark green, green, yellow-brown, green-brown

facts.text: Coarse green celadon (nokcheongja) has a body with sand and other impurities, many pores, and a green-brown, uneven glaze similar to ash glaze; it served ordinary people.
facts.quote_gloss: its colour holds a green-brown tinge

facts.text: Early celadon kilns already fired good wares inside saggars (갑발).
facts.quote_gloss: saggar

facts.text: Early celadon began under the influence of Yue ware from Zhejiang, at kilns on the west and south-west coasts.
facts.quote_gloss: under the influence of Yue celadon from Zhejiang, China

examples.title: 청자 '순화4년'명 항아리 (celadon jar dated 993) — earliest dated whole Korean celadon; inscription covered by the dating agent

rows.name: Goryeo celadon, plain ('kingfisher-color' bisaek celadon)
rows.period: Goryeo (peak first half of the 12th century)
kilns: Daegu-myeon, Gangjin County, South Jeolla: Sadang-ri (Dangjeon village), Yongun-ri, Gyeyul-ri, Sudong-ri; Samheung-ri, Chilyang-myeon (encykorea now writes the province as 전남광주통합특별시)
Yucheon-ri, Boan-myeon and Jinseo-myeon, Buan County, North Jeolla (전북특별자치도)
rows.what_it_is: Celadon decorated, if at all, only by its shape or light carving, admired for its gray-green 'kingfisher' glaze (bisaek, 翡色). The Song envoy Xu Jing praised it in 1123, and the group from King Injong's tomb (d. 1146) shows the style at its height.
how_to_recognize: Body: fine pale-gray, iron-bearing clay (not white), so the glaze reads as a gray-based green.

Glaze: thin, even gray-green to blue-green, translucent to slightly milky; the best early-12th-century glaze has almost no crackle, but many 12th-century items show a fine net of crackle, so crackle alone does not date an item.
Color faults: where the kiln oxidised, the same pot can be part green and part yellow or brown — common on genuine items.

Foot and supports: small, neatly trimmed foot; small fine items fired on small silica (quartz) spurs that leave small white spur marks on the foot; large items fired on spurs of refractory clay mixed with sand.
Forms: melon-shaped vases, maebyeong (plum vases), ewers with lids, lobed bowls and cups, many copying metalwork.

copies.text: Gangjin, the main Goryeo kiln district, is today the center of modern celadon production and of revivals of Goryeo styles.
Korean sources give no simple test for telling a modern copy; the period features above (body color, glaze, spur marks, foot trimming) are what the sources describe for genuine Goryeo items.

facts.text: Goryeo people called the color of their celadon bisaek (翡色, 'kingfisher color').
facts.quote_gloss: the people of Goryeo called it bisaek

facts.text: Xu Jing, a Song envoy at Gaeseong in 1123, wrote that Goryeo potters' work had lately become more skilful and its color finer, and compared Goryeo wares with Yue and Ru celadons.
facts.quote: 근래에 들어 제작기술이 정교해지고 빛깔이 더욱 좋아졌다
facts.quote_gloss: lately the technique has become refined and the colour even better

facts.text: Celadon body: white clay with a little iron under a feldspathic glaze containing about 1–3% iron; the body fires a pale gray, so the overall color is a gray-based green.
facts.quote_gloss: the body colour is a pale grey

facts.text: The bisaek glaze completed in the first half of the 12th century was semi-opaque with almost no crackle; from the mid-12th century the glaze grew clearer and more items show crackle.
facts.quote: 반실투성(半失透性)의 빙렬(氷裂)이 거의 없는
facts.quote_gloss: semi-opaque, with almost no crackle

facts.text: 12th-century plain and incised celadons carry crackle as recorded in official descriptions (net-like crackle on the former NT 97 maebyeong; slight crackle on the former NT 169 bamboo bottle), so crackle is not by itself a sign of a late or fake item.
facts.quote: 표면에 그물 모양의 빙렬(氷裂)이 있다
facts.quote_gloss: there is net-shaped crackle on the surface

facts.text: Small, ordinary items of the peak period were fired on silica (quartz) spurs, leaving small white spur marks on a small, neat foot.
facts.quote_gloss: fired propped on silica-sand spurs

facts.text: The silica spur marks are small and look white.
facts.quote_gloss: the silica-spur scars look small and white

facts.text: Large vessels were fired on spurs of refractory clay mixed with sand; Yun notes refractory-clay spur scars in the glaze of larger bottles and jars.
facts.quote_gloss: fired on refractory-clay/sand spurs

facts.text: Where the fire was oxidising, celadon turned yellow or brown, and a substantial number of items are green on one part and brownish on another.
facts.quote_gloss: on the same vessel one part is kingfisher green and another…

facts.text: Firing temperature of Goryeo celadon: Jeong gives about 1,250–1,300 °C; the Met essay gives 'commonly around, or below, 1150ºC'.

The celadons from King Injong's tomb (Jangneung, d. 1146), found with a book dated 皇統六年 (1146), are the reference group for plain bisaek celadon of the first half of the 12th century; matching sherds come from Sadang-ri kilns 7 and 8, Gangjin.
facts.quote_gloss: Huangtong year 6 (1146)

examples.title: 청자 참외모양 병 (melon-shaped vase), from King Injong's tomb, first half 12th c.
Six-lobed bowl, early 12th century
Vase in the Form of a Melon, 1100s

rows.name: Goryeo celadon with incised or carved (relief) decoration
rows.hanja: 陰刻靑磁 · 陽刻靑磁
kilns: Sadang-ri, Daegu-myeon, Gangjin, South Jeolla
Yucheon-ri, Boan-myeon, Buan, North Jeolla
rows.what_it_is: Celadon decorated by cutting into the clay before glazing: incised lines (eumgak) or carved-away backgrounds that leave the design in low relief (yanggak), under the usual gray-green glaze.
how_to_recognize: Decoration cut into the body under the glaze: fine 'thread-like' incised lines, or broader carving leaving lotus petals, peonies, parrots or bamboo in relief.
Same body, glaze and foot as plain celadon (pale-gray body, gray-green glaze, silica spurs on small items).
Forms: maebyeong, kundika (Buddhist water sprinklers), ewers, bowls.

facts.text: From the late 11th to early 12th century contacts with Chinese kilns (Yaozhou, Ding, Cizhou and others) brought incised, relief and mold-impressed decoration to Goryeo celadon, which became Goryeo in style.
facts.quote_gloss: incised, relief and mould-pressed decoration

facts.text: The former NT 97 incised lotus maebyeong (H. 43.9 cm) has a clear pale green-gray glaze with net crackle and is attributed by its glaze and shape to the Sadang-ri kilns, Gangjin, 12th century.
facts.quote: 사당리 가마에서 구워 냈을 것으로 추정
facts.quote_gloss: thought to have been fired at the Sadang-ri kilns

examples.title: 청자 음각연화당초문 매병 (maebyeong with incised lotus scroll), 12th c.
청자 양각죽절문 병 (bottle with bamboo in relief), 12th c.
Gourd-shaped ewer decorated with waterfowl and reeds, early 12th c., carved and incised
Water Ewer for Rituals (Kundika) with Incised Parrot Design, 1100s
examples.note: label text describes the bird as a phoenix

rows.name: Goryeo celadon with openwork, and sculptural (figure-shaped) celadon
rows.hanja: 透刻靑磁 · 象形靑磁
kilns: Gangjin (Daegu-myeon), South Jeolla
Buan, North Jeolla
rows.what_it_is: Pierced (openwork) decoration and vessels modelled as lions, fish-dragons, ducks, melons or figures — the most technically demanding Goryeo celadons, made mainly for the court and temples.
how_to_recognize: Openwork: designs cut right through the wall (e.g. the ball-shaped lid of the NMK incense burner), often combined with small white or black slip dots.

Sculptural forms: incense burners with lion or animal lids, ewers in the form of fish-dragons or tortoise-dragons, water droppers; eyes marked with dots of iron-black slip; teeth and fins sometimes touched with white slip.
Glaze: gray-green bisaek with soft lustre.

facts.text: Xu Jing (1123) singled out a lion-topped incense burner (狻猊出香) as also bisaek and the most finely made of Goryeo wares.
facts.quote_gloss: the suanni (lion) incense burner is also bisaek

facts.text: Openwork (투각) was among the techniques that mid-Goryeo potters took from China and made their own, alongside copper-red and marbled wares.
facts.quote_gloss: openwork technique skilfully handled

facts.text: The NMK openwork incense burner (former NT 95) combines a pierced ball with white dots at the crossings, a chrysanthemum-leaf bowl and a base held up by three rabbits whose eyes are black dots.
facts.quote: 구형 부분 곳곳의 교차 지점에는 흰 점
facts.quote_gloss: white dots at the crossing points of the ball

examples.title: 청자 투각칠보문뚜껑 향로 (incense burner with openwork lid), 12th c.
청자 사자형뚜껑 향로 (incense burner with lion lid), first half 12th c.
청자 어룡형 주전자 (fish-dragon ewer), 12th c.

rows.name: Goryeo celadon with mold-impressed decoration
rows.hanja: 壓出陽刻靑磁 · 陽印刻
kilns: Gangjin, South Jeolla
Buan, North Jeolla
rows.what_it_is: Bowls, dishes and cups shaped over a carved mold, which pressed a relief design (lotus scrolls, peonies, fish, phoenixes) into the inside. The method came from the Yaozhou kilns in Shaanxi and allowed standardised production.
how_to_recognize: Crisp, repeated low-relief design on the inside of bowls and dishes, often with a lobed or flower-shaped rim.
Some items combine a molded inside with inlay on the outside.
Same body, glaze and spur practice as other Goryeo celadon.

facts.text: Mould-pressing (압출양각) began at the Yaozhou kilns in Shaanxi, reached Goryeo around the late 11th century and was used vigorously until about the mid-13th century; it made standardised production possible.
facts.quote: 틀을 이용하여 문양과 형태를 찍어내는 방법
facts.quote_gloss: a method of pressing pattern and shape with a mould

facts.text: A bowl with silver-mounted rim (former NT 253) has its inside lotus scroll pressed in relief and peonies inlaid on the outside — the only recorded item mixing the two styles in this way.
facts.quote_gloss: lotus scroll stamped in relief

examples.title: 청자 양각연화당초상감모란문 은테 발 (bowl, moulded inside, inlaid outside, silver rim)
청자 양각연지어문 화형 접시 (flower-shaped dish, moulded lotus pond and fish)
Celadon Cup with Molded Lotus Petal Design, 1100s–1200s
Celadon Dish with Molded Phoenix Design in the Shape of a Flower, 1200s
Cup with handle, 13th c., inlaid and molded

rows.name: Goryeo inlaid celadon (sanggam)
rows.period: Goryeo (mid-12th century to 1392; decline from the late 13th, steep in the late 14th)
kilns: Sadang-ri (Dangjeon village) and Gyeyul-ri, Daegu-myeon, Gangjin, South Jeolla
Yucheon-ri, Boan-myeon, Buan, North Jeolla (more inlaid celadon than Gangjin in the later 12th c., per nikh)
rows.what_it_is: Celadon whose designs — cranes and clouds, chrysanthemums, willows and waterfowl — are cut into the clay and filled with white and black slip before glazing. It is the type the West most associates with Goryeo; the Met calls it a rarity in China.
how_to_recognize: Design lines and areas filled with white slip and black (iron-rich) slip, sealed under the celadon glaze; 'reverse inlay' fills the background with white and leaves the motif in the body color.
Typical motifs: cranes and clouds in roundels, chrysanthemum sprays, willow-and-waterfowl scenes, lotus-petal and 'thunder' borders at foot and shoulder.
12th–13th c. items: clear gray-green glaze, fine inlay, small trimmed foot, silica or refractory-clay spurs as on other celadon.
Later 13th c. (ganji-dated 1269–1287 group): dull dark-green clouded glaze, heavier shapes, coarse and simplified inlay, clumsier foot, sand supports beginning.
14th c.: thin yellowish-brown or grayish-green glaze with fine crackle, glaze roughly scraped off the foot, fired on sand in most cases; decline of the inlay leads into early buncheong.

copies.text: Modern revivals: Gangjin county's 1977 revival committee built a wood-fired kiln and in February 1978 first succeeded in reproducing Goryeo celadon with natural glaze; Icheon (Gyeonggi) potters such as Yu Geun-hyeong also reproduced Goryeo celadon after 1945 (see post1945_celadon_revival).
No source found that gives connoisseurship tests for telling colonial-era 'Korai' or modern reproductions from Goryeo items; see gaps.

facts.text: Inlay: the design is cut into the dry clay body and the cuts are filled with black and/or white slip before the translucent glaze is applied and fired.
facts.quote: filling in the carved space with black and/or white slip

facts.text: The bowl from the tomb of Mun Gong-yu (d. 1159) is the earliest dated inlaid celadon; its inside uses reverse inlay (background filled with white slip).
facts.quote: 연대를 알 수 있는 상감청자 가운데 가장 오래된
facts.quote_gloss: the oldest among inlaid celadons whose date is known

facts.text: Dating of inlay: Jeong puts the emergence of inlay in the first half of the 12th century and its peak in the mid-12th century; nikh says inlay was tried in small amounts from the 10th century, grew in share from the later 12th century, and that most surviving inlaid wares date to the 13th–14th centuries. Yun Yong-i (1992) re-dates several cyclically dated items 60–120 years later than earlier readings.
facts.quote_gloss: from the later 12th century its share gradually grew

facts.text: Celadons with ganji dates of 1269–1287 show dull glaze, slack curves, rough and simplified inlay, and sand supports beginning to appear on the foot.
facts.quote_gloss: sand supports begin to appear

facts.text: Mid/late 14th-century inlaid dishes (the junghae 丁亥, c.1347 group) have yellowish-brown, thinly crackled glaze; the foot was roughly scraped after glazing and sand supports were used in most cases.
facts.quote: sand supports were used in most cases

facts.text: In the later 12th century more inlaid celadon was made in Buan than in Gangjin; inlaid celadon is rare at provincial kilns.
facts.quote: 강진보다도 부안 일대에서 더 많은 상감청자가 제작
facts.quote_gloss: more inlaid celadon was made around Buan than Gangjin

facts.text: Inlaid celadon is a rarity in China (Met); nikh notes the inlay method itself is first known from the Huangbao kiln in Shaanxi, but only Goryeo made it a main decoration.

examples.title: 청자 상감운학문 매병 (maebyeong with inlaid cranes and clouds), 12th c. 2nd half
청자 상감연지원앙문 정병 (kundika with inlaid lotus pond and mandarin ducks), 12th c.
청자 상감당초문 완 (bowl from the tomb of Mun Gong-yu, d. 1159)
Maebyeong decorated with cranes and clouds, second half 12th c.
Maebyeong decorated with cranes and clouds, late 13th c.
Oil bottle with reverse-inlaid peony leaves, late 12th c.
Vase with Inlaid Lotus, Plum, and Bamboo Design, late 1300s (label: grey-green glaze, declining inlay)

rows.name: Goryeo iron-painted celadon
rows.period: Goryeo (10th–13th century; most surviving items 12th c.)
kilns: Haenam kilns, South Jeolla (Cleveland label; single source)
Gangjin and Buan (iron-decorated sherds among kiln finds)
rows.what_it_is: Celadon painted under the glaze with iron-rich slip in bold brown-black brushwork — willows, plants, scrolls — closer in spirit to Chinese Cizhou ware than to the refined inlaid wares.
how_to_recognize: Brown-black painting in iron pigment under the glaze; bold, loose brushwork of willows, grasses, scrolls.
Glaze often fired in oxidation, so olive, yellowish or brownish rather than gray-green; the same item may be part green by chance.
Forms: dish-mouthed long-necked bottles, hourglass drums (janggo), maebyeong, cylindrical bottles.
Foot: on the Leeum maebyeong (Treasure former no. 1383), the inside of the foot is cut away and coarse sand traces remain on the resting surface.

facts.text: Iron-painted celadon was painted with iron-bearing slip and celadon-glazed; most items were fired in oxidation and so are yellow-brown, with bold, thick-lined designs; forms and designs resemble Northern Song Cizhou ware.
facts.quote_gloss: oxidation-fired, yellow-brown

facts.text: Iron painting was used for simple scrolls and plant designs on dish-mouthed bottles, hourglass drums and maebyeong.
facts.quote_gloss: on dish-mouthed bottles, janggo drums, maebyeong…

facts.text: The Leeum iron-painted maebyeong (Treasure former no. 1383) has its foot hollowed out and traces of coarse sand on the resting surface.
facts.quote_gloss: traces of coarse sand under the resting surface

facts.text: A Cleveland iron-painted bottle is attributed to the Haenam kilns in southern Jeolla.
Iron-painted (철화) designs appear on celadon from the 10th century, alongside white-slip dot decoration (퇴화).
facts.quote: 철화문(鐵畫文) 및 퇴화문(堆花文)도 나타나기 시작한다
facts.quote_gloss: iron-painted and white-dotted designs also begin to appear

examples.title: 청자 철화양류문 통형 병 (cylindrical bottle with iron-painted willows)
청자 철화초충조문 매병 (maebyeong with iron-painted plants, insects, birds), 12th c.
Vase with Floral Design, 1100s, celadon with underglaze iron-brown
Arhat, 13th–14th c., iron-brown decoration under celadon glaze

rows.name: Goryeo celadon with copper-red decoration
rows.hanja: 銅畵靑磁 · 辰砂靑磁
kilns: Gangjin (copper-red sherds among Daegu-myeon kiln finds), South Jeolla
rows.what_it_is: Celadon touched or painted with copper oxide, which turns red in a reducing kiln. Usually a small accent — petal tips on inlaid peonies — and rarely, as on the Leeum gourd ewer, a bold painted design.
how_to_recognize: Red to crimson accents (often petal tips, small dots) set into inlaid designs; rarely, whole leaf outlines painted in red.
Copper red is hard to control and tends to bleed (nikh).
Otherwise the usual celadon body, glaze and foot.

facts.text: Copper oxide painted under the glaze turns red when fired in reduction; Goryeo potters used it sparingly, as accents.
facts.quote_gloss: bright red from copper oxide pigment in reduction firing

facts.text: Copper-red accents: the NMK maebyeong (Treasure former no. 346) has copper red inlaid at the tips of its inlaid peony petals.
facts.quote: 모란꽃잎 끝에 붉은 안료를 상감해 넣었다
facts.quote_gloss: red pigment inlaid at the tips of the peony petals

facts.text: Copper oxide is hard to control because it bleeds.
facts.quote_gloss: copper oxide, limited by its tendency to bleed

facts.text: Start date: the official description of the Leeum gourd ewer says copper red was used in the first half of the 12th century but bold copper-red designs appear from the 13th century (the ewer is from the tomb of Choe Hang, d. 1257, Ganghwa); Yun dates the start of copper red to the later 12th century; Jeong puts it among mid-12th-century techniques.
facts.quote_gloss: existed already in the first half of the 12th century

facts.text: Korean sources (Jeong; Yun) state that Goryeo potters were the first in the world to use copper red on ceramics, two centuries ahead of China. This claim is reported, not checked.
facts.quote_gloss: more than two centuries ahead of China

examples.title: 청자 동화연화문 표주박모양 주전자 (gourd-shaped ewer with copper-red lotus), from the tomb of Choe Hang
청자 상감동채모란문 매병 (maebyeong with inlaid and copper-red peonies), 13th c.
Oil bottle decorated with peonies and chrysanthemums, 13th c., copper-red and inlaid

rows.name: Goryeo gold-painted (gilt) celadon
kilns: Gangjin, South Jeolla, or Buan, North Jeolla (Jeon 2012 thinks Gangjin more likely; Buan possible)
rows.what_it_is: Inlaid (or plain) celadon with gold added along the outlines of its designs, made for a few patrons and as gifts to the Yuan court. Very few survive, and the gold is usually worn or lost.
how_to_recognize: Gold applied along the edges of inlaid motifs; the fired surface was scratched along the outlines with a sharp tool and the scratches filled with gold paste.
Very few survive (encykorea names three: two at the NMK, one in a Japanese private collection); Jo In-gyu told Khubilai the gold is lost when the vessel breaks.
Shapes and inlay match contemporary late-13th-century inlaid celadon: wide-mouthed flattened bottles, thick walls, pale blue-green glaze, dense small flowers, motifs in lozenge-shaped panels.

facts.text: Technique: outlines of the finished celadon's designs were scratched with a sharp tool and filled with gold paste.
facts.quote: 무늬 가장자리 선을 따라 예리한 도구로
facts.quote_gloss: along the edge lines of the design with a sharp tool

facts.text: Goryeosa records gold-painted celadon presented to the Yuan: Jo In-gyu's exchange with Khubilai (who told Goryeo not to gild porcelain because the gold is lost when it breaks) and a 1297 gift of 金畵甕器 to the Yuan emperor.
facts.quote_gloss: gold-painted onggi (vessels)

facts.text: From the two Goryeosa records, gold-painted celadon was being produced in 1289 and 1297; its designs and techniques otherwise match contemporary inlaid celadon.
Start date: Kang dates gilt celadon to the late 13th–early 14th century; Jeong thinks a very few were made from the first half of the 12th century.
facts.quote_gloss: from the late 13th to the first half of the 14th century

examples.title: 청자상감화금수하원무늬편호 (flattened jar with inlaid and gilt monkeys under a tree)
Small jar and cover decorated with chrysanthemums, cranes, and clouds, late 13th c., gold and inlaid

rows.name: Goryeo white porcelain
rows.period: Goryeo (from the 10th century; style continues in provincial kilns into the 15th)
kilns: Seo-ri, Idong-myeon, Yongin, Gyeonggi (early, with halo-foot bowls)
Jungam-ri, Yeoju, Gyeonggi
Yucheon-ri, Boan-myeon, Buan, North Jeolla (12th-c. inlaid and carved white)
Seoksu-dong, Anyang, Gyeonggi (late 14th c.)
rows.what_it_is: A small production of white wares beside celadon — a tiny fraction of Goryeo output. Most is softer and less vitrified than later Joseon porcelain, and some is inlaid like celadon.
how_to_recognize: Body: often soft, coarse, plaster-like in the 11th c.; better fused in the 12th c.
Glaze: thin, often with fine crackle, and frequently flaking away from the body because the two did not bond — a common feature of Goryeo-type white.
Color: beige-tinged or faintly bluish white; early items have halo feet like early celadon.
Decoration: incised, carved, molded, black inlay (sometimes celadon-clay inlay), iron painting.
Caution: Chinese white and bluish-white (qingbai) wares were imported in quantity and are found in Korean tombs; a Cleveland cup given as a rare Goryeo white item proved to be Song Chinese.

facts.text: Goryeo white was a tiny fraction of production — not even a few hundredths of celadon, per Jeong; nikh calls early white a minor, very small production.
facts.quote_gloss: only very small amounts were produced

facts.text: 11th-century Goryeo white has a weak, plaster-like body and very thin glaze that often did not bond and has flaked off.
facts.quote_gloss: there are many examples where the glaze has fallen away

facts.text: Inlaid white porcelain of the mid-12th century comes mainly from the Yucheon-ri kilns at Buan; Goryeo inlay on white used black clay and sometimes celadon clay.
facts.quote: 부안군 보안면 유천리 가마가 그 대표적인
facts.quote_gloss: the Yucheon-ri kiln at Boan-myeon, Buan, is the representative one

facts.text: Chinese ceramics — mostly white wares, also qingbai, black Jian bowls and Cizhou-type wares — are found in Korean sites; a Cleveland cup donated as rare Goryeo 'white celadon' turned out to be Song Chinese.
facts.quote: turns out to be an imported Song period Chinese example

examples.title: 백자 상감모란문 매병 (white maebyeong with inlaid peonies), Goryeo mid-12th c. (encykorea 백자 상감)
Floral-shaped Cup with Incised Chrysanthemum Design, 1100s–1200s (label: bluish-white ware of white clay)
Bowl, catalogued as Song Chinese after being donated as Goryeo white (caution example)

rows.name: Goryeo black- and iron-glazed wares
rows.hanja: 黑釉 · 鐵釉 · 鐵彩
kilns: Undae-ri, Duwon-myeon, Goheung, South Jeolla (early black glaze)
Daegu-myeon, Gangjin, South Jeolla (iron-slip and black-glaze sherds with celadon)
rows.what_it_is: Dark wares made beside celadon: vessels covered in iron slip under a clear glaze (cheolchae, glossy near-black), iron glazes, and black glazes, sometimes with white inlaid or slip-painted designs such as ginseng leaves.
how_to_recognize: Near-black to dark brown surface from iron slip or glaze on a celadon-type body.
White designs scraped or inlaid through the dark slip, or painted on in white slip (e.g. ginseng leaves).
Caution: Chinese black Jian tea bowls were imported in Goryeo.

facts.text: Gangjin's Daegu-myeon kilns yield sherds of iron-painted, copper-red, iron-slip, iron-glazed, black-glazed and white wares besides celadon.
facts.quote: 철채(鐵彩) · 철유(鐵釉) · 흑유(黑釉)
facts.quote_gloss: iron-slip, iron glaze, black glaze

facts.text: The NMK iron-slip maebyeong (Treasure former no. 340): iron slip over a celadon body, motif areas thinly cut away and painted with white slip; such wares are rare, and sherds collected at Gangjin suggest they were made with ordinary celadon.
facts.quote_gloss: collected at the Daegu-myeon kilns, Gangjin

facts.text: A small amount of black-glazed ware was made early, at Undae-ri, Goheung.
facts.quote_gloss: black-glazed ware too, in a particular area

examples.title: 청자 철채퇴화삼엽문 매병 (iron-slip maebyeong with white ginseng leaves), 12th c.
Iron-glazed Prunus Vase with Inlaid Floral Design, 1100s–1200s

rows.name: Buncheong with inlaid decoration
kilns: Kilns all over the peninsula; stamped and inlaid wares especially in Gyeongsang, sgraffito and incised wares in Jeolla, iron-painted wares at Gyeryongsan (Hakbong-ri, Banpo-myeon, Gongju, South Chungcheong); a key 15th-c. site is Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (Jeolla).
Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (inlaid sherds of the mid-15th c.)
rows.what_it_is: The first buncheong: Goryeo-style inlay carried on, with looser, livelier designs and a duller glaze. In the earliest items it is hard to tell from early Joseon inlaid celadon.
how_to_recognize: Black-and-white inlaid lines, and from the mid-15th c. broad area inlay (면상감).
Often combined with stamped bands (e.g. chrysanthemum stamps on the neck of the NMK dragon jar).
Forms: maebyeong with flaring mouth and S-curved profile, jars, bottles, flasks.

Body: gray to gray-black stoneware like late celadon but coarser and darker; a thin, transparent glaze — pale bluish gray-white or faintly yellowish — lets the gray body show through where there is no white slip.
Everything decorative is done with white slip (분장 粉粧) on that dark body: stamped, inlaid, incised, scraped, brushed, painted over, or dipped.

copies.text: Buncheong was revived in Japan by descendants of Korean potters settled there and by Japanese potters; Western museums hold Japanese tea bowls in buncheong manner (e.g. Met 93.1.94, Kyoto ware with inlaid and stamped design, probably 2nd half 17th c.; Met 36.120.518 'Gohon (Korean-style)' tea bowl, 18th c.). Western catalogues sometimes use Japanese trade names: Cleveland labels a 13th-c. Goryeo oil bottle 'painted celadon (Mishima ware)', and encykorea glosses brushed slip as 刷毛目 (Japanese hakeme). How specialists separate Japanese from Korean items is not stated in the sources read.

facts.text: Buncheong: a gray or gray-black body coated with refined white slip, glazed and fired in reduction; the name is short for 粉粧灰靑沙器 (bunjang hoecheong sagi).
facts.quote_gloss: a grey or grey-black body

facts.text: The name bunjang hoecheong sagi was coined in the 1930s by Go Yu-seop; the ware had no name of its own in contemporary documents.
The glaze is thin and transparent, slightly bluish gray-white or slightly yellowish, so the gray body shows clearly through it.
facts.quote_gloss: the colour of the grey body (shows) through the glaze

facts.text: Buncheong was made for about 200 years (15th–16th c.); it was absorbed into white porcelain from the later 16th century and was not made again after the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598.
facts.quote_gloss: after the Imjin War it was not made again

facts.text: Inlaid buncheong descends directly from Goryeo inlaid celadon and is hard to distinguish from early Joseon inlaid celadon.
facts.quote_gloss: hard to distinguish from early-Joseon inlaid celadon

facts.text: Inlay appears all over the country in the early Joseon; items of the mid–late 15th century with area inlay (면상감) are fresh and robust.
facts.quote_gloss: works with area inlay

facts.text: Buncheong maebyeong differ from Goryeo maebyeong: the mouth flares and the profile curves in an S from shoulder to foot.
facts.quote_gloss: an S-shaped curve

examples.title: 분청사기 상감운룡문 항아리 (jar with inlaid clouds and dragons), first half 15th c.
Bottle Inlaid with Peony and Scroll Design, 1400s

rows.name: Buncheong with stamped decoration (inhwa)
kilns: Kilns all over the peninsula; stamped and inlaid wares especially in Gyeongsang, sgraffito and incised wares in Jeolla, iron-painted wares at Gyeryongsan (Hakbong-ri, Banpo-myeon, Gongju, South Chungcheong); a key 15th-c. site is Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (Jeolla).
rows.what_it_is: Small stamps — chrysanthemum heads, rings, petals — pressed in rows into the clay, filled with white slip and wiped, giving dense, regular white patterns. Many dishes and bowls also carry the names of government offices or districts.
how_to_recognize: Dense, regular rows of tiny white stamped motifs (chrysanthemum the commonest; also butterflies, rings, lotus petals, ruyi heads).
Peak (Sejo reign, 1455–1468): the whole surface filled, motifs in orderly bands; late (16th c.): stamps shallow, sometimes no slip, slip brushed on and not wiped.
Forms: bowls, dishes, jars, placenta jars.

Body: gray to gray-black stoneware like late celadon but coarser and darker; a thin, transparent glaze — pale bluish gray-white or faintly yellowish — lets the gray body show through where there is no white slip.
Everything decorative is done with white slip (분장 粉粧) on that dark body: stamped, inlaid, incised, scraped, brushed, painted over, or dipped.
