facts.text: Stamped technique: motifs are stamped, the surface is covered with white slip and wiped, leaving white slip in the stamped hollows — a kind of inlay.
facts.quote: 도장으로 찍은 뒤 백토로 분장하고 닦아내면
facts.quote_gloss: stamped, slip-covered and wiped

facts.text: Stamped buncheong is found everywhere but was most developed in Gyeongsang (Yeongnam), with fine, dense patterns.
facts.quote_gloss: stamped ware is distributed nationwide, but…

facts.text: Under Sejo (1455–1468) stamped decoration reaches its most refined form.
facts.quote_gloss: stamped decoration shows its greatest refinement

facts.text: In the 16th century stamping becomes shallow and may be left without white slip, or thin brushed slip is left unwiped under the glaze.
facts.quote_gloss: the stamping becomes very shallow

examples.title: 분청사기 인화국화문 태항아리 (placenta jars, inner and outer, stamped chrysanthemums), 15th c.
Dish with inscription and decorated with chrysanthemums and rows of dots, mid-15th c.
Bowl with inscription and chrysanthemums and tortoiseshell decoration, mid-15th c.

rows.name: Buncheong with sgraffito (scraped-away background) decoration (bakji)
kilns: Kilns all over the peninsula; stamped and inlaid wares especially in Gyeongsang, sgraffito and incised wares in Jeolla, iron-painted wares at Gyeryongsan (Hakbong-ri, Banpo-myeon, Gongju, South Chungcheong); a key 15th-c. site is Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (Jeolla).
rows.what_it_is: The pot is covered with white slip, a design is drawn, and the slip around the design is scraped away, so a white motif stands on the dark body. Bold peonies, lotus and fish; a Jeolla speciality.
how_to_recognize: White motif left standing in slip against scraped-back dark gray body (sometimes the background is also painted with iron to sharpen the contrast).
Drawn outlines (incised) combined with scraping; motifs peony, lotus, fish.
Forms: flattened bottles (pyeonbyeong), 'turtle' flasks (jarabyeong), jars, janggun (barrel-shaped flasks).

Body: gray to gray-black stoneware like late celadon but coarser and darker; a thin, transparent glaze — pale bluish gray-white or faintly yellowish — lets the gray body show through where there is no white slip.

facts.text: Sgraffito (박지): after slipping and drawing the design, the slip of the background is scraped away, leaving a white design on the dark body.
facts.quote_gloss: after scraping away the background around the design

facts.text: Sgraffito and incised buncheong developed above all in Jeolla.
facts.quote: 전라도에서는 독특한 조형과 미감을 보이는 조화나 박지기법
facts.quote_gloss: in Jeolla, incised or sgraffito techniques with a distinctive look

facts.text: A sgraffito urn found in the stupa of the monk Gobong (d. 1430) at Songgwangsa shows the technique was in use before 1430.
facts.quote_gloss: since the monk Gobong died in 1430

examples.title: 분청사기 박지연화어문 편병 (flattened bottle, sgraffito lotus and fish), 15th c.
분청사기 박지철채모란문 자라병 (turtle flask, sgraffito peony with iron-painted ground), late 15th c.
Bowl decorated with peony leaves and chrysanthemum, 15th c., sgraffito and stamped
Wine Flask with Incised and Sgraffito Peony Design, 1500s

rows.name: Buncheong with incised decoration (johwa)
kilns: Kilns all over the peninsula; stamped and inlaid wares especially in Gyeongsang, sgraffito and incised wares in Jeolla, iron-painted wares at Gyeryongsan (Hakbong-ri, Banpo-myeon, Gongju, South Chungcheong); a key 15th-c. site is Chunghyo-dong, Gwangju (Jeolla).
rows.what_it_is: A design scratched through the white slip with a pointed tool, so it shows as dark lines on white. Fish, lotus and abstract patterns, drawn fast and freely; most common in Jeolla.
how_to_recognize: Dark gray lines on a white slipped ground (the opposite of sgraffito's white-on-dark).
Free, quick drawing: smiling fish, lotus, birds, abstract lines.
Forms: bottles, flattened bottles, jars.

Body: gray to gray-black stoneware like late celadon but coarser and darker; a thin, transparent glaze — pale bluish gray-white or faintly yellowish — lets the gray body show through where there is no white slip.

rows.name: Joseon white porcelain, plain
rows.date_note: Jeong's periods: early 1392–1649/50, middle 1650/51–1751, late 1752–end of Joseon.
kilns: Official (court) kilns of the Saongwon branch office (Bunwon) in Gwangju, Gyeonggi — moved about every ten years: 15th–16th c. Beoncheon-ri, Ojeon-ri (Namhansanseong-myeon), Doma-ri, Usan-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Jeongji-ri (Toechon-myeon), Mugap-ri, Hakdong-ri (Chowol); 17th c. Tanbeol-dong, Sangnim-ri, Seondong-ri, Songjeong-dong, Yusa-ri, Sindae-ri; early 18th c. Ohyang-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Geumsa-ri (Namjong-myeon); from 1752 Bunwon-ri (Namjong-myeon)
15th-c. upper-grade white also listed at Sangju and Goryeong (North Gyeongsang) in the Sejong sillok jiriji; provincial kilns everywhere from the 16th c.
rows.what_it_is: Undecorated white porcelain, the ware the Joseon court and elite preferred above all; over 90% of white ware was plain from the later 16th century. Grades were made side by side: saggar-fired royal wares and stacked, coarser wares for offices and the market.
how_to_recognize: Early (15th–16th c.), royal grade: snowy white with a faint blue tinge, glaze slightly thick and nearly uncrackled, fired in saggars on fine sand; foot often cut as an inverted triangle.
Early, office / lower grade: pale bluish or light-gray white, often fine crackle, 'bamboo-joint' foot (jukjeol-gup), fired stacked on three to six spurs of body clay or grit (taeto bijim).
17th c.: grayish-white glaze; feet cruder; coarse sand supports; peripheral kilns made concave-footed (ommok-gup) gray wares on coarse sand.
Early 18th c. (Geumsa-ri): milky 'snow white' with faint blue, often a net of crackle; fine sand; new faceted shapes.
Late (Bunwon-ri, from 1752): bluer, thicker, very hard glaze without crackle and with many bubbles; thick walls and wide, deeply cut feet; sand supports, refractory-clay supports at the very end.
Caution: late bluish white is sometimes mistaken for 'qingbai'; Japanese machine-made porcelain flooded Korea from the late 19th century.

copies.text: From the late 19th century machine-made white wares from Kyushu (Japan) — thick, hard, smooth and without variation of line — flooded Korea, and Japanese-owned factories in Korea produced the same kind.

facts.text: From the later 16th century Joseon ceramics were almost all white porcelain, and over 90% of it undecorated.
facts.quote_gloss: plain white porcelain was over 90%

facts.text: Early-Joseon upper-grade white was fired in saggars on fine sand, with a slightly thick, almost uncrackled, faintly blue glaze.
facts.quote_gloss: fired on fine sand supports

facts.text: Royal white wares are snowy white with an inverted-triangle foot, fired in saggars on sand; wares for government offices are pale blue or light gray, with a bamboo-joint foot, fired stacked on body-clay spurs.
facts.quote_gloss: inverted-triangle foot, with sand as the support material

facts.text: Lower-grade early white often keeps throwing marks, has bamboo-joint feet and was fired on body-clay spurs.
facts.quote_gloss: fired on body-clay spurs

facts.text: After the Imjin War the foot, once neatly finished, became cruder and fine sand gave way to coarse sand supports, continuing into the early 17th century.
facts.quote_gloss: changed to firing on coarse sand

facts.text: 17th-century peripheral kilns around the court kilns made gray, impure 'concave-foot' white wares fired on coarse sand; 17th-c. sites (Tanbeol, Hakdong, Sangnim, Seondong, Yusa, Sindae) made much iron-painted ware.
facts.quote_gloss: concave-foot white ware on coarse sand

facts.text: Middle-period (Geumsa-ri) white has very faint blue, often a net-like crackle, and fine sand on a vertical foot.
facts.quote_gloss: often has net-like crackle

facts.text: Late (Bunwon-ri) white is bluer than earlier wares, dense, with no crackle and many bubbles; walls and feet are thick and wide.
facts.quote_gloss: the glaze has no crackle and many bubbles

facts.text: At the end of the Bunwon period refractory-clay supports were used instead of sand.
facts.quote_gloss: at the end, refractory-clay supports are used

facts.text: Late white is so bluish that some people wrongly take it for 'blue-white' (qingbai).
facts.quote_gloss: some misunderstand it as qingbai

facts.text: The court kilns at Gwangju began in the 1460s; scholars place the founding between 1466 and 1469 (Jeon Seungchang: about 1466; Yun Yong-i: about 1467; Kim Young-won: 1467–68; Kang Kyung-sook: after 1469).
facts.quote_gloss: the official kiln was set up in Gwangju between 1466 and 1468

rows.name: Joseon blue-and-white porcelain
rows.hanja: 靑畵白磁 · 靑華白磁
kilns: Official (court) kilns of the Saongwon branch office (Bunwon) in Gwangju, Gyeonggi — moved about every ten years: 15th–16th c. Beoncheon-ri, Ojeon-ri (Namhansanseong-myeon), Doma-ri, Usan-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Jeongji-ri (Toechon-myeon), Mugap-ri, Hakdong-ri (Chowol); 17th c. Tanbeol-dong, Sangnim-ri, Seondong-ri, Songjeong-dong, Yusa-ri, Sindae-ri; early 18th c. Ohyang-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Geumsa-ri (Namjong-myeon); from 1752 Bunwon-ri (Namjong-myeon)
18th–19th c. also provincial kilns
rows.what_it_is: White porcelain painted under the glaze in cobalt blue. For two centuries it was a rare court luxury, because cobalt (回回靑, 'Muslim blue') had to be bought from China; it became abundant only after the Bunwon settled at Bunwon-ri in 1752.
how_to_recognize: Cobalt blue under a clear glaze on white porcelain.
15th–16th c.: few, fine items; Ming-influenced at first, then spare painterly pines, bamboo, plum, birds painted by court painters with much empty space.
17th c.: blue almost absent (cobalt unobtainable); iron-brown used instead.
First half 18th c. (Geumsa-ri): spare sprays of autumn grasses, orchids, pinks, irises; faceted bottles and jars.
Late 18th–19th c. (Bunwon-ri): much more blue-and-white; auspicious motifs, characters 壽 and 福, folk-painting style, often combined with iron and copper red; stationery and ritual vessels.
Color of the blue: imported cobalt (containing arsenic) versus domestic 'earth blue' (iron and manganese rich — blackish or grayish-purple); the difference can be judged by eye only partly.

copies.text: Ming blue-and-white came to Korea as imperial gifts (e.g. 1430) and Chinese polychrome porcelain was imported and admired; whether the blue-and-white wine jar drawn in the Sejong sillok ritual volume is Chinese or Korean is disputed.

facts.text: Blue-and-white reached Korea in the late 14th century and Korean production began about the mid-15th century (Kang; Jeong: imported from the Sejong reign and then fired with imported cobalt), at first strongly influenced by Ming, distinctively Korean by the later 15th century.
facts.quote_gloss: seems to be about the mid-15th century

facts.text: Cobalt (回回靑 / 回靑) was imported from China; when it could not be had, 'earth blue' (土靑) was sought in Korea between 1463 and 1469.
facts.quote_gloss: between 1463 and 1469

facts.text: Chemically, imported cobalt contains arsenic, domestic 'earth blue' much iron and manganese (iron gives a dark blackish tone, manganese grayish-purple); surviving items cannot be clearly sorted, and by eye only partly.
facts.quote: 육안으로 어느 정도 구별이 가능할 뿐이다
facts.quote_gloss: can be distinguished by eye only to some degree

facts.text: The earliest dated Korean blue-and-white is the jar dated 弘治二年 (1489) at Dongguk University Museum.
facts.quote_gloss: a work of 1489 (Seongjong 20)

facts.text: Court painters (화원) were sent each year to the kilns to paint the royal wares, so Joseon blue-and-white follows contemporary painting styles.
facts.quote: 每歲司饔院官率畫員 監造御用之器
facts.quote_gloss: every year a Saongwon official leads court painters to supervise the making of royal wares

facts.text: In the 17th century cobalt could hardly be obtained (war damage, then anti-Qing feeling), so iron-brown took the place of blue for court use.
facts.quote_gloss: iron-painted white ware took its place

facts.text: Geumsa-ri (first half 18th c.) blue-and-white has spare grasses and flowers — pinks, irises, chrysanthemums, orchids — and new faceted forms.
facts.quote_gloss: pinks, irises, chrysanthemums, orchids

facts.text: After the Bunwon settled at Bunwon-ri, blue-and-white production rose rapidly; late wares are popular, with folk-painting motifs and auspicious designs.
facts.quote_gloss: folk-painting style patterns appear clearly

rows.name: Joseon white porcelain with iron-brown painting
rows.period: Joseon (late 15th c. on; flourishing in the 17th c.)
kilns: Official (court) kilns of the Saongwon branch office (Bunwon) in Gwangju, Gyeonggi — moved about every ten years: 15th–16th c. Beoncheon-ri, Ojeon-ri (Namhansanseong-myeon), Doma-ri, Usan-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Jeongji-ri (Toechon-myeon), Mugap-ri, Hakdong-ri (Chowol); 17th c. Tanbeol-dong, Sangnim-ri, Seondong-ri, Songjeong-dong, Yusa-ri, Sindae-ri; early 18th c. Ohyang-ri, Gwaneum-ri, Geumsa-ri (Namjong-myeon); from 1752 Bunwon-ri (Namjong-myeon) — 17th c. especially Sangnim-ri (from the 1630s), Seondong-ri, Jeongji-ri
Provincial kilns (e.g. 17th-c. iron-brown kilns at Yongyeon-ri, Damyang, South Jeolla, and Jeongsaeng-dong, Daejeon)
rows.what_it_is: White porcelain painted under the glaze with iron oxide (seokganju), which fires brown to black. Made from the late 15th century, it became the main painted ware in the 17th century when cobalt was unobtainable — dragons, bamboo, plum, grapes, grasses, in bold, often humorous brushwork.
how_to_recognize: Brown to brown-black (sometimes reddish-brown) painting; iron spreads and drags, so tones are hard to grade and lines are heavy.
17th c.: grayish-white glaze, cloud-dragon jars, bamboo and plum; foot often hollowed concave and fired on fine (court) or coarse (peripheral) sand.
Regional kilns: loose, comic dragons on round jars.
Late 18th–19th c.: iron rarely alone, mostly used with blue and copper red.

facts.text: Iron-painted white porcelain began in the later 15th century, was produced in small amounts in the 15th–16th centuries, and reached its distinctive beauty in the mid-17th century.
facts.quote_gloss: radiates a distinctive beauty in the mid-17th century

facts.text: Iron-brown appears at the court kilns from the Sangnim-ri kiln of the 1630s and continues through the mid–late 17th century; in 1634 dragons were painted in seokganju on jars for receiving envoys.
facts.quote_gloss: appears from the Sangnim-ri kiln of the 1630s

facts.text: Seokganju (石間朱) is an iron-oxide mineral pigment found in many places in Korea; on white porcelain it fires brown or reddish-brown, spreads, and drags on the brush, so gradations are hard.
facts.quote_gloss: mostly brown or reddish-brown

facts.text: Iron-brown became popular from the 17th century, especially when cobalt was very expensive or uneven; court items are refined, while regional kilns painted carefree dragons on round jars.

The Ewha iron-painted cloud-dragon jar (Treasure former no. 645) has a concave hollowed foot with fine-sand marks and grayish glaze, features found at the 17th-c. Gwangju kiln sites of Sangnim-ri, Seondong-ri and Jeongji-ri.
facts.quote: 가는 모래 받침을 받쳐 구운 흔적
facts.quote_gloss: traces of firing on fine sand

facts.text: From the late 18th century iron is mostly used together with blue; on its own it is very rare.
facts.quote_gloss: examples of independent use are very rare

백자 철화운룡문 항아리 (jar with cloud dragon), 17th c.

rows.name: Joseon white porcelain with copper-red decoration
rows.hanja: 辰砂白磁 · 銅畵白磁
rows.period: Joseon (securely from the later 17th c.; mainly 18th–19th c.)
kilns: Gwangju court kilns (Geumsa-ri, Bunwon-ri), Gyeonggi
Provincial kilns in Gyeonggi; Yeongheung County, South Hamgyeong (North Korea) — sherds found
rows.what_it_is: White porcelain painted with copper oxide, which fires red in reduction — hard to control, so rarer than blue or iron. Court items combine red with blue and iron; provincial jars and faceted bottles use red alone in bold sprays of bamboo, lotus, grapes or pine and crane.
how_to_recognize: Red painting under the glaze in copper (the 1684 epitaph dishes are described as vermilion-tinged on a grayish-white ground).
Court wares: red together with cobalt blue and iron-brown, sometimes with molded relief.
Provincial wares: round jars and faceted bottles with red alone, bold and free; 19th c. small angled or tall jars with simple red motifs.
Rare variant: whole surface washed red with a reserved white relief design.

facts.text: The earliest securely dated Joseon copper-red items are three epitaph dishes dated 1684 (崇禎後甲子) in the National Museum of Korea; copper red was in use on white porcelain by the later 17th century at the latest.
facts.quote_gloss: inscribed 'gapja after Chongzhen' (1684)

facts.text: Copper-red white porcelain was hard to make: copper needs a higher firing temperature and is more volatile than cobalt or iron.
facts.quote_gloss: it was hard to get good results

facts.text: Successful copper-red items date primarily to the 18th century (Met); Yun says copper red was made at the Bunwon and at provincial kilns in the 18th–19th centuries, in small demand.
facts.quote: dating primarily to the eighteenth century

facts.text: At the court kilns copper red was almost never used alone but with blue, sometimes with iron too; provincial kilns painted round jars and faceted bottles with copper red alone.
facts.quote: 진사와 청화 안료가 함께 사용된 예가 많으며
facts.quote_gloss: there are many examples using copper red and cobalt together

facts.text: Copper-red sherds are known from the Bunwon-ri court kiln and from folk kilns in Yeongheung, South Hamgyeong; 19th-century small copper-red jars are thought to come from Gyeonggi provincial kilns rather than Gwangju.
facts.quote_gloss: folk kilns in the Yeongheung area, South Hamgyeong

examples.title: 백자 청화철채동채초충문 병 (bottle with relief orchid, chrysanthemum and insects in blue, iron and copper red), first half 18th c., Gwangju
Jar with grapevine decoration, mid-18th c., underglaze copper red

rows.name: Moon jar (large round white jar)
rows.hanja: 白磁大壺 (official hanja now 白磁 壺)
rows.period: Joseon (late 17th – mid-18th century, above all c.1700–1750; made on into the 19th)
rows.date_note: KHS: about a century from the late 17th to the early 18th c., especially the first fifty years of the 18th; Met dates its jar to the second half of the 18th c.; V&A dates its jar 1800–1900 and calls moon jars 18th–19th c.; encykorea says by the 19th c. most households had one.
kilns: Gwangju court kilns, Gyeonggi — above all Geumsa-ri (Namjong-myeon), also Bunwon-ri
rows.what_it_is: A large, nearly spherical white porcelain jar, usually over 40 cm high, thrown in two halves — top and bottom — and joined at the middle. The milky-white color and slightly irregular round shape suggested the full moon, hence the name.
how_to_recognize: Size: usually more than 40 cm high (Busan Museum's is over 50 cm); body diameter about equal to height; short, outward-slanting mouth and a foot of about the same diameter as the mouth.
Construction: upper and lower halves thrown separately and joined; a seam or slight step at the widest point; often lopsided or leaning — not a fault.
Color: milky white (yubaek), cream, snowy or faintly gray or bluish; glaze can pool or melt poorly near the base.
Base: glaze wiped from the foot ring; fired on fine sand; the clay shrinks about 20% in firing.
Unpainted (an iron-painted dragon variant exists).

copies.text: Contemporary Korean potters make moon jars as studio works (V&A: Kim Syyoung 2019, FE.202-2019; Ryu Jongdae 2023, FE.42-2024); Ju Sekyun's 'Tracing Drawing' series imitates designated National Treasures in white stoneware. Sources read give no test for separating a late copy from an 18th-century jar.

facts.text: Moon jars are usually over 40 cm high; their round, milky-white form recalls the full moon, hence the alias 'dal hangari' (moon jar).
facts.quote_gloss: a name given because it resembles the full moon

facts.text: Because of their size they could not be thrown in one item: upper and lower halves were made separately and joined, so many are asymmetrical and show the joint.
facts.quote: 상하 부분을 따로 만든 후, 두 부분을 접합하여
facts.quote_gloss: after making the upper and lower parts separately, joining the two

facts.text: Most were made at the court kilns at Gwangju, chiefly at Geumsa-ri, from the late 17th to the early 18th century, especially in the first half of the 18th century.
facts.quote: 금사리 가마에서 주로 제작된 것으로 추정
facts.quote_gloss: thought to have been made mainly at the Geumsa-ri kiln

facts.text: Round jars became 'moon jars' — mouth, foot, maximum width and height roughly equal — towards the late 17th century; small ones held food, large ones served as ritual flower vessels or for display.
facts.quote_gloss: changed into the so-called moon jar

facts.text: The 1991 National Treasure jar: milky-white glaze evenly applied, glaze wiped from the foot and fired on fine sand; join mark at the middle of the body.
facts.quote_gloss: fired propped on fine sand

facts.text: Joseon white porcelain shrinks about 20% in the kiln, so the 50 cm+ Busan jar was thrown about 65 cm high.
facts.quote_gloss: since it generally shrinks by about 20%

facts.text: Name: designations once called these jars 백자대호 (large white jar); the 1991 National Treasure is called 백자대호 in an encykorea entry, while current KHS names are 백자 달항아리 (with hanja 白磁 壺).
facts.quote_gloss: the white large jar designated National Treasure in 1991

facts.text: Moon jars spread from limited production in the middle Joseon to ordinary households by the 19th century.
facts.quote: 어느 가정에서나 한 개쯤 있는 친숙한 세간
facts.quote_gloss: a familiar household item, one in every home

facts.text: The Met's moon jar (1979.413.1) is 38.7 cm high and dated to the second half of the 18th century; the Met essay says moon jars became fashionable in the 18th century.

rows.name: Late Joseon court-kiln porcelain of the Bunwon-ri period
rows.hanja: 分院里 白磁 (分院 沙器)
rows.period: Late Joseon (1752 – 1884, privatised kiln to the 1900s)
kilns: Bunwon-ri, Namjong-myeon, Gwangju, Gyeonggi — on the Han River where the North and South Han meet (site now under a school, damaged in the colonial period)
rows.what_it_is: After 1752 the court kiln stopped moving and stayed at Bunwon-ri, so 'Bunwon ware' usually means late Joseon court porcelain: hard, bluish white wares, much more blue-and-white, many scholar's desk items, ritual vessels, bottles and jars. In 1884 the kiln was handed to merchant-contractors and lost out to Japanese and Chinese imports.
how_to_recognize: Bluish, hard, dense glaze without crackle; thick walls and wide feet; sand supports.
Many stationery items (brush holders, often openwork; water droppers), ritual vessels, faceted and molded items.
Blue-and-white dominant; blue with iron and copper red; auspicious motifs and characters in the 19th century.

facts.text: The court kiln moved roughly every ten years in search of firewood until 1752, when it was fixed at Bunwon-ri, convenient for water transport where the North and South Han rivers meet.
facts.quote_gloss: moved to Bunwon-ri in spring 1752 (Yeongjo 28)

facts.text: Geumsa-ri, the court kiln before Bunwon-ri: c.1720/1721–1752 per Yun and nikh; Kim Kyoung-joong (2022) puts the Gwaneum-ri no.19 area at 1721–1733 and Geumsa-ri at 1734–1751.
facts.quote_gloss: Geumsa-ri (1734–1751)

facts.text: End of the court kiln: 1882 (Kang), 1883 (Jeong; Yun in 광주 요지; Ju In-taek; Im Eung-geuk), or 1884 (Yun in 관요; nikh/Bang Byeong-seon, citing the 1884 regulations 分院磁器貢所節目, which turned it into a contractor-run 'gongso' still supplying the court). The Met says the 1880s.
facts.quote_gloss: changed into the Bunwon gongso in 1884

facts.text: Bunwon-ri produced mostly stationery, ritual vessels, bottles and jars, with bluish white glaze; most surviving late white and blue-and-white wares were made there.
facts.quote: 문방구, 제기, 병, 호 등이 많이 제작되었다
facts.quote_gloss: many stationery items, ritual vessels, bottles and jars were made

facts.text: Saggar-fired top-grade ware (gapbeon), meant for the court, was by 1793 used for tableware even by commoners despite repeated bans.
facts.quote_gloss: even the lowly (used) saggar wares

facts.text: After 1884: the contractors failed; c.1897 a porcelain company (燔磁會社) with Seoul capital took over, and in 1895 a Japanese set up a kiln in Korea and supplied wares for a state funeral.
facts.quote_gloss: in 1895 a Japanese even set up a kiln in Joseon

examples.title: Openwork jar with peonies, late 18th–early 19th c.

rows.name: Provincial (folk) porcelain and brown-glazed wares, 18th–19th century
rows.hanja: 地方窯 白磁 · 民窯 · 石間硃
kilns: Provincial kilns of Gyeonggi and other provinces; Yeongheung, South Hamgyeong (copper red)
rows.what_it_is: Porcelain made outside the court kiln for the growing market: thicker, grayer white wares with free painting in iron, copper red or blue, and dark-brown glazed (seokganju) jars and bottles for storage.
how_to_recognize: Copper-red painting alone on round jars, faceted bottles, small angled or tall jars — simple, bold or naive.
Iron-brown dragons and plants painted loosely on round jars.
Seokganju (石間硃): dark brown to black-brown iron glaze, often on faceted jars and bottles — storage vessels of late Joseon.
Caution: from the late 19th century Japanese and Chinese imported porcelain circulated widely; Japanese machine-made Kyushu wares are thick, hard, smooth and uniform in line.

facts.text: Provincial kilns painted round jars and faceted bottles with copper red alone; 19th-century angled and small tall jars with naive copper-red motifs are thought to come from Gyeonggi provincial kilns, not Gwangju.
facts.quote: 지방가마에서는 둥근 항아리와 각병(角甁)에 진사로만
facts.quote_gloss: provincial kilns use copper red alone on round jars and faceted bottles

facts.text: Seokganju (dark-brown black-glazed) jars and bottles, mostly faceted, were made from the end of the middle period and much used in late Joseon as storage vessels.
facts.quote_gloss: much used as storage vessels in late Joseon

facts.text: From the late 19th century machine-made Japanese (Kyushu) porcelain — thick, hard, smooth, with no variation in line — flooded Korea; Japanese and Chinese imports circulated ever more widely.
facts.quote_gloss: mass-produced by machine

examples.title: Jar, 1800–1850, underglaze blue roundels

rows.name: Onggi (brown-glazed earthenware storage jars)
rows.period: Late Joseon to the present (glazed onggi from the 17th century)
kilns: Everywhere; 17th-c. finds at the iron-brown porcelain kilns of Yongyeon-ri, Damyang (South Jeolla) and Jeongsaeng-dong, Daejeon; Mapo and Noryangjin (Seoul) named as pot-making places in the early Joseon
rows.what_it_is: Everyday earthenware coated with a yellow-brown glaze (yakto) — kimchi and soy jars, steamers, water jars, chamber pots, barrel flasks. Porous walls 'breathe', which suits fermentation.
how_to_recognize: Coarse earthenware with a yellow-brown glaze (yakto); walls porous ('breathing vessel').
Forms: soy and kimchi jars (jangdok), water jars, rice jars, steamers (siru), water-carrying jars (dongi), vinegar bottles, barrel flasks (janggun), chamber pots.
20th c.: red lead (gwangmyeongdan, 光明丹) glaze used from the colonial period and widely after the 1960s.
Colonial-era liquor-brewery jars may be incised with capacity and inspection words such as 第 號 石 斗 年 月 檢定.

facts.text: Onggi: earthenware coated with a yellow-brown glaze called yakto (藥土); the term covers jars, steamers, vinegar bottles, chamber pots and many other glazed household vessels.
facts.quote: 약토(藥土)라는 황갈색의 유약을 입힌 질그릇
facts.quote_gloss: earthenware coated with the yellow-brown glaze called yakto

facts.text: Yellow-brown glazed onggi has not been found at 15th–16th-century kiln sites but appears at 17th-century iron-painted porcelain kilns (Damyang Yongyeon-ri, Daejeon Jeongsaeng-dong), so glazed onggi seems to begin after the 1592–1637 wars.
facts.quote_gloss: 17th-century iron-painted white porcelain kiln sites

facts.text: Red lead (光明丹, lead oxide) began to be used on onggi under Japanese rule and was widely used from the 1960s.
facts.quote_gloss: gwangmyeongdan (lead oxide)

facts.text: Colonial-era liquor jars from licensed breweries carry characters for number, capacity and inspection (第·號·石·數·斗·幷·年·月·檢定), sometimes a cyclical date or the brewery name.
facts.quote_gloss: inspection (passed)

facts.text: In the early Joseon Seong Hyeon's Yongjae chonghwa names Mapo and Noryangjin as places making earthenware jars.
facts.quote: 마포, 노량진 등지에서는 진흙 굽는 것을 업으로
facts.quote_gloss: at Mapo, Noryangjin and so on, firing clay is the trade

rows.name: Colonial-period ceramics (1910–1945): Japanese factories and 'Korai' (Goryeo-style) reproductions
kilns: Seoul: Hanyang Goryeo-so (漢陽高麗燒), Goryeo-style ceramics made for the retailer Haesi Sanghoe in the 1910s–20s
Busan: Japan Hard Pottery (日本硬質陶器) factory from 1917
Mokpo (Haengnamsa, 1942), Miryang (1942), Bucheon and Daegu (1943)
rows.what_it_is: After the court kiln closed, Japanese porcelain and Japanese-run factories in Korea took over the market, while workshops such as Hanyang Goryeo-so in Seoul made 'Goryeo-style' (高麗燒) ceramics for retailers. The Gangjin Goryeo kilns were found and surveyed in these same years (1913–14). Their makers' marks are in the inscriptions explorer.
how_to_recognize: Factory wares: machine-thrown or molded, thick, smooth, uniform.
Goryeo-style celadon of this period exists, but the sources read give no physical tests for separating it from Goryeo items.

copies.text: Goryeo-style celadon was made commercially in the colonial period (e.g. Hanyang Goryeo-so for Haesi Sanghoe, 1910s–20s). No source read states how to tell such items from Goryeo originals.

facts.text: In 1917 the Japanese company Japan Hard Pottery set up a factory in Busan with modern kilns and mechanical wheels; by 1945 there were 16 ceramics factories in Korea (9 in the south, 7 in the north).
facts.quote_gloss: 16 ceramics factories in operation

facts.text: The Seoul retailer Haesi Sanghoe had its ceramics made by Hanyang Goryeo-so (漢陽高麗燒) in the 1910s–20s.
facts.quote_gloss: Hanyang Goryeo-so

facts.text: After the Bunwon closed, the flood of Japanese ceramics nearly cut the Korean tradition; reproducing celadon became a matter of national pride.
facts.quote_gloss: with the flood of Japanese ceramics

facts.text: The Sadang-ri kiln site at Gangjin became known in 1913 when a Japanese policeman found celadon sherds; the Yi Royal Household Museum surveyed it the next year, and Gangjin was listed as a historic site in 1939.
facts.quote_gloss: the next year the Yi Royal Household Museum surveyed the site

rows.name: Post-1945 celadon and porcelain revival (Icheon, Gangjin)
kilns: Sindun-myeon, Icheon, Gyeonggi (e.g. Yu Geun-hyeong 'Haegang', Ji Sun-tak, Jo So-su)
Daegu-myeon, Gangjin, South Jeolla (Gangjin county kiln from 1977; Gangjin Celadon Museum workshops)
Gwangju (Jeolla): Mudeung-yo of Jo Gi-jeong (1966 on)
rows.what_it_is: Studios and county workshops that set out to reproduce Goryeo celadon and Joseon white wares after liberation — a local in Icheon recalls Japanese visitors buying up pottery by the hundreds each week after the 1965 Korea–Japan treaty. Their makers' marks are in the inscriptions explorer.
how_to_recognize: Makers' marks: see the inscriptions explorer.
Quality ranges from cheap souvenirs to fine studio work; side by side, glaze color and precision of pattern differ (Nakamura).

copies.text: These are the modern reproductions that most often stand in for Goryeo celadon in Western homes; the sources read do not give connoisseurship tests beyond marks and the period features listed under each Goryeo ware.

facts.text: In Icheon (Sindun-myeon) Yu Geun-hyeong, Ji Sun-tak, Jo So-su and others reproduced Goryeo celadon and Joseon white porcelain around two surviving kilns after the war; Yu (Haegang) is said to have restored Goryeo celadon in 1959.
facts.quote_gloss: achieved its restoration in 1959

facts.text: Gangjin county formed a Goryeo celadon reproduction committee in 1977, built a wood-fired 'Gangjin official kiln' and in February 1978 first succeeded in reproducing Goryeo celadon with natural glaze.
facts.quote: 천연유약을 사용한 고려청자 재현사업을 국내 최초로 성공
facts.quote_gloss: first in Korea to succeed in reproducing Goryeo celadon with natural glaze

facts.text: Modern Goryeo-style celadon is sold everywhere in Korean souvenir shops, from very cheap cups to expensive items; seen side by side, they differ in glaze color and accuracy of design.
facts.quote: 並べてみると、その釉薬の色合いから模様の正確さ
facts.quote_gloss: placed side by side, from the glaze colour to the accuracy of the pattern…

tried from the 10th c.; share grows from the later 12th c.; most surviving inlaid wares 13th–14th c.
several cyclically dated items should be re-dated 60–120 years later

stamped decoration from the later 7th c. (unification); continued into the 9th c.
